[Joe Biden](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden")'s tenure as the [46th](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States "List of presidents of the United States") [president of the United States](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") began with [his inauguration](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inauguration_of_Joe_Biden "Inauguration of Joe Biden") on January 20, 2021, and ended on January 20, 2025. Biden, a member of the [Democratic Party](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"), had previously served as the [47th vice president from 2009 to 2017](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_presidency_of_Joe_Biden "Vice presidency of Joe Biden") under President [Barack Obama](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"), took office after defeating the [Republican](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") incumbent president [Donald Trump](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") in the [2020 presidential election](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election "2020 United States presidential election"). Upon his inauguration, he became the [oldest president in American history](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_age "List of presidents of the United States by age"), breaking the record set by [Ronald Reagan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan").[[1]](#cite_note-1) Alongside Biden's presidency, the Democratic Party also held their majorities in the [House of Representatives](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") and the [Senate](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") during the [117th U.S. Congress](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/117th_United_States_Congress "117th United States Congress") following the [2020 elections](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_elections "2020 United States elections"), thereby attained an overall federal [government trifecta](about://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_trifecta#United_States "Government trifecta"). Biden entered office amid the [COVID-19 pandemic](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"), an [economic crisis](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "Economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"), and increased [political polarization](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_polarization_in_the_United_States "Political polarization in the United States").[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Day one actions of his presidency included restoring U.S. participation in the [Paris Agreement](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Agreement "Paris Agreement"), revoking the permit for the [Keystone XL](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keystone_XL "Keystone XL") pipeline and halting funding for the [Mexico–United States border wall](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico–United_States_border_wall "Mexico–United States border wall").[[3]](#cite_note-Everett-2022-3) On his second day, he issued a series of executive orders to reduce the impact of [COVID-19](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19"), including invoking the [Defense Production Act of 1950](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_Production_Act_of_1950 "Defense Production Act of 1950"), and set an early goal of achieving one hundred million [COVID-19 vaccinations](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_vaccine "COVID-19 vaccine") in the United States in his first 100 days.[[4]](#cite_note-Klein-2021-4) The first major legislation signed into law by Biden was the [American Rescue Plan Act of 2021](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Rescue_Plan_Act_of_2021 "American Rescue Plan Act of 2021"), a $1.9 trillion [stimulus bill](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stimulus_(economics) "Stimulus (economics)") that temporarily established expanded unemployment insurance and sent $1,400 stimulus checks to most Americans in response to continued economic pressure from COVID-19.[[5]](#cite_note-5) He signed the bipartisan [Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrastructure_Investment_and_Jobs_Act "Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act"), a ten-year plan brokered by Biden alongside Democrats and Republicans in Congress to invest in American roads, bridges, public transit, ports and broadband access.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Biden proposed a significant expansion of the U.S. social safety net through the [Build Back Better Act](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Build_Back_Better_Act "Build Back Better Act"), but those efforts, along with [voting rights legislation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_to_Vote_Act "Freedom to Vote Act"), failed in Congress. In August 2022, Biden signed the [Inflation Reduction Act of 2022](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation_Reduction_Act_of_2022 "Inflation Reduction Act of 2022"), a domestic appropriations bill that included some of the provisions of the Build Back Better Act after the entire bill failed to pass. It included significant federal investment in climate and domestic clean energy production, tax credits for solar panels, electric cars and other home energy programs as well as a three-year extension of [Affordable Care Act](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act") subsidies, an [insulin](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insulin_(medication) "Insulin (medication)") price cap, and a provision allowing [Medicare](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_(United_States) "Medicare (United States)") to negotiate drug prices. In late 2022, Biden signed the [Respect for Marriage Act](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respect_for_Marriage_Act "Respect for Marriage Act"), which repealed the [Defense of Marriage Act](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_of_Marriage_Act "Defense of Marriage Act") and codified [same-sex](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_marriage "Same-sex marriage") and [interracial](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interracial_marriage "Interracial marriage") marriage in the United States. ealth care for US veterans; the [Electoral Count Reform and Presidential Transition Improvement Act](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_Count_Reform_and_Presidential_Transition_Improvement_Act_of_2022 "Electoral Count Reform and Presidential Transition Improvement Act of 2022"); and the [Juneteenth National Independence Day Act](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juneteenth "Juneteenth"), making Juneteenth a [federal holiday in the United States](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_holidays_in_the_United_States "Federal holidays in the United States"). Biden also unsuccessfully pushed for legislation protecting the right to [abortion](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion "Abortion") in response to the [U.S. Supreme Court](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States")'s decision in *[Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobbs_v._Jackson_Women's_Health_Organization "Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization")* overturning *[Roe v. Wade](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roe_v._Wade "Roe v. Wade")*.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Biden appointed [Ketanji Brown Jackson](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ketanji_Brown_Jackson "Ketanji Brown Jackson") to the [U.S. Supreme Court](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Supreme_Court "U.S. Supreme Court")—the first [Black woman](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_women "Black women") to serve on the court. In response to the [debt-ceiling crisis of 2023](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_United_States_debt-ceiling_crisis "2023 United States debt-ceiling crisis"), he negotiated and signed the [Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiscal_Responsibility_Act_of_2023 "Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023"), which restrains federal spending for fiscal years 2024 and 2025, implements minor changes to [SNAP](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supplemental_Nutrition_Assistance_Program "Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program") and [TANF](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temporary_Assistance_for_Needy_Families "Temporary Assistance for Needy Families"), includes energy permitting reform, claws back some [IRS](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_Revenue_Service "Internal Revenue Service") funding and unspent money for [COVID-19](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"), and suspended the [debt ceiling](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_debt_ceiling "United States debt ceiling") to January 1, 2025.[[9]](#cite_note-9) He established the [American Climate Corps](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Climate_Corps "American Climate Corps") and created the first ever [White House Office of Gun Violence Prevention](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House_Office_of_Gun_Violence_Prevention "White House Office of Gun Violence Prevention"). On September 26, 2023, Biden visited a [United Auto Workers](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Auto_Workers "United Auto Workers") picket line during the [2023 United Auto Workers strike](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_United_Auto_Workers_strike "2023 United Auto Workers strike"), making him the first US president to visit one. Biden also rigorously enforced antitrust laws by appointing [Lina Khan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lina_Khan "Lina Khan") to head the [FTC](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Trade_Commission "Federal Trade Commission").[[10]](#cite_note-Khan-10) Biden issued more individual pardons and commutations than any other president,[[11]](#cite_note-APpardons-11) including controversial sweeping pardons of members of his family and high-profile political figures that he claimed were either presently or expected to be the subject of "baseless and politically motivated investigations."[[12]](#cite_note-cnbc.com-12)[[13]](#cite_note-bbc.com-13)[[14]](#cite_note-cnn.com-14) The first sitting U.S. president to oppose the [death penalty](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment_in_the_United_States "Capital punishment in the United States"), Biden commuted the sentences of nearly all inmates on federal death row to [life imprisonment](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_imprisonment "Life imprisonment") weeks before leaving office.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

The foreign policy goal of the Biden administration was to restore the U.S. to a "position of trusted leadership" among global [democracies](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy "Democracy") in order to address the challenges posed by [Russia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia") and [China](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"). Biden signed [AUKUS](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AUKUS "AUKUS"), an international security alliance together with [Australia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia") and the [United Kingdom](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"). He supported the expansion of [NATO](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO") with the additions of [Finland](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland "Finland") and [Sweden](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden "Sweden"). Biden approved a raid which led to the death of [Abu Ibrahim al-Hashimi al-Qurashi](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Ibrahim_al-Hashimi_al-Qurashi "Abu Ibrahim al-Hashimi al-Qurashi"), the leader of the [Islamic State](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_State "Islamic State"), and approved a drone strike which [killed Ayman Al Zawahiri](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killing_of_Ayman_al-Zawahiri "Killing of Ayman al-Zawahiri"), leader of Al-Qaeda. He completed the [withdrawal of U.S. military forces from Afghanistan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020–2021_U.S._troop_withdrawal_from_Afghanistan "2020–2021 U.S. troop withdrawal from Afghanistan"), declaring an end to [nation-building](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nation-building "Nation-building") efforts and shifting U.S. foreign policy toward strategic competition with China and, to a lesser extent, Russia.[[16]](#cite_note-ShearTankersley-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18) During the withdrawal, the [Afghan government collapsed and the Taliban seized control](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Taliban_offensive "2021 Taliban offensive"), leading to Biden receiving bipartisan criticism. He responded to the [Russian invasion of Ukraine](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine") by imposing [sanctions on Russia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_sanctions_during_the_2022_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "International sanctions during the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine") and providing Ukraine with over $100 billion in [combined military, economic, and humanitarian aid](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_military_aid_to_Ukraine_during_the_Russo-Ukrainian_War "List of military aid to Ukraine during the Russo-Ukrainian War").[[19]](#cite_note-19)[[20]](#cite_note-20) During the [Gaza war](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war "Gaza war"), Biden condemned the actions of [Hamas](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamas "Hamas") and other Palestinian militants as terrorism, and announced [American military support](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_support_for_Israel_in_the_Gaza_war "United States support for Israel in the Gaza war") for [Israel](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel"); he also sent humanitarian aid to the [Gaza Strip](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_Strip "Gaza Strip") and brokered a [four-day temporary pause and hostage exchange](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Gaza_war_ceasefire "2023 Gaza war ceasefire") in 2023 followed by a [three-phase ceasefire](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_2025_Gaza_war_ceasefire "January 2025 Gaza war ceasefire") in January 2025. Biden negotiated and oversaw the [2024 Ankara prisoner exchange](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Ankara_prisoner_exchange "2024 Ankara prisoner exchange"), the largest [prisoner exchange](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoner_exchange "Prisoner exchange") since the end of the [Cold War](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War"), involving the release of 26 individuals, including American journalist [Evan Gershkovich](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Gershkovich "Evan Gershkovich") and former U.S. Marine [Paul Whelan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Whelan "Paul Whelan").

Biden began his term with over 50% approval ratings; these fell significantly after the withdrawal from Afghanistan,[[21]](#cite_note-21) and remained low as the country experienced high inflation and rising gas prices, even as they later decreased during his presidency.[[22]](#cite_note-22)[[23]](#cite_note-23) His [age and mental fitness](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_and_health_concerns_about_Joe_Biden "Age and health concerns about Joe Biden") were a frequent subject of discussion throughout his presidency,[[24]](#cite_note-24) ultimately culminating in his decision to [withdraw](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Withdrawal_of_Joe_Biden_from_the_2024_United_States_presidential_election "Withdrawal of Joe Biden from the 2024 United States presidential election") his bid for re-election in the [2024 presidential election](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election "2024 United States presidential election").[[25]](#cite_note-25) Trump won the election against Biden's preferred successor, [Kamala Harris](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris"), making him the second U.S. president to be succeeded in office by his predecessor.[[a]](#cite_note-26) Biden oversaw the strongest economic recovery of any [G7 nation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G7 "G7") post COVID-19 and one of the strongest economic recoveries in United States history, breaking a 70-year record for low unemployment,[[26]](#cite_note-27) and the creation of over 16 million new jobs, the most of any single term president.[[27]](#cite_note-28) During Biden's time in office, median [wages](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wage "Wage") stagnated,[[28]](#cite_note-:1-29) and the share of [wealth](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wealth_inequality_in_the_United_States "Wealth inequality in the United States") of the wealthiest 0.1% of Americans continued to increase.[[29]](#cite_note-:2-30)

Political scientists and historians have largely [rated](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_rankings_of_U.S._Presidents "Historical rankings of U.S. Presidents") Biden's presidency unfavorably.[[30]](#cite_note-31) Historian [Julian E. Zelizer](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_E._Zelizer "Julian E. Zelizer") described Biden as unable to provide effective leadership or overcome [political polarization](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_polarization_in_the_United_States "Political polarization in the United States") during his presidency.[[31]](#cite_note-32)[*[page needed](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")*] Biden was the first president since Republican [George H. W. Bush](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush") to serve only one full term, and the first Democrat since [Jimmy Carter](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") to do so.[[32]](#cite_note-33) His political legacy is interwoven with the re-election of Trump in 2024.[[33]](#cite_note-legacyNeg1-34)

## Milestones

**AUKUS** ( [*AW-kəs*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")), also styled as **Aukus**, is a trilateral security partnership between [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"), the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), and the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), which have stated that its goals are to "promote a free and open [Indo-Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Pacific "Indo-Pacific") that is secure and stable."[[1]](#cite_note-:8-1) Initially announced on 15 September 2021, the partnership involves two lines of effort referred to as pillars.[[2]](#cite_note-Announce-2)[[3]](#cite_note-CRSR47599-3) Pillar 1 focuses on Australia acquiring [nuclear-powered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_submarine "Nuclear submarine") [attack submarines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_submarine "Attack submarine") and the rotational basing of US and UK nuclear-powered attack submarines in Australia.[[4]](#cite_note-4) Pillar 2 entails the collaborative development of advanced capabilities in six technological areas: undersea capabilities, [quantum technologies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_technology "Quantum technology"), [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") and autonomy, advanced [cyber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberwarfare "Cyberwarfare"), [hypersonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersonic_weapon "Hypersonic weapon") and [counter-hypersonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missile_defense "Missile defense") capabilities, and [electronic warfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_warfare "Electronic warfare"); and in two broader functional areas: innovation and information sharing.[[5]](#cite_note-FactSheet-5)[[3]](#cite_note-CRSR47599-3)

AUKUS is widely seen as a response to the perception among its members that the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") poses a threat to the Indo-Pacific region.[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) The Chinese government said, when the partnership was announced, that it risked "severely damaging regional peace" and had a "[cold-war mentality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Cold_War "Second Cold War")".[[8]](#cite_note-8)

A direct result of the creation of the partnership was Australia's controversial cancellation of a French-Australian [submarine contract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack-class_submarine "Attack-class submarine") worth [€](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro "Euro")56 billion ([A$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_dollar "Australian dollar")90 billion).[[9]](#cite_note-recall-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) The Australian government only gave the French government a few hours' notice of this before the public announcement of AUKUS.[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-ABC17Sep2021-12) The Australian government agreed to a €555 million ([US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar")584 million) compensation settlement with French defence contractor [Naval Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Group "Naval Group").[[13]](#cite_note-CNN2022-13)[[14]](#cite_note-AJ2022-14)

### Naval Group–Australia strategic partnership agreement

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=AUKUS&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Naval Group–Australia strategic partnership agreement")]

In 2009, two years after the start of the project to replace the [Royal Australian Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Australian_Navy "Royal Australian Navy")'s [conventionally-powered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine#Diesel%E2%80%93electric_transmission "Submarine") [*Collins*-class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collins-class_submarine "Collins-class submarine") submarines, the Australian Defence White Paper stated: "The Government has ruled out nuclear propulsion for these submarines".[[15]](#cite_note-15)

In 2016, [Prime Minister of Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Australia "Prime Minister of Australia") [Malcolm Turnbull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_Turnbull "Malcolm Turnbull") signed a A$50 billion (€31 billion) deal with the majority French government-owned company [Naval Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Group "Naval Group") (known as DCNS until 2017) to design a new generation of submarines, known as the [*Attack* class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack-class_submarine "Attack-class submarine"), under the "Future Submarine Program", scheduled to replace the *Collins* class.[[16]](#cite_note-ABC-15-sep-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[note 1]](#cite_note-21) The design was based on the latest French nuclear-powered [attack submarine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_submarine "Attack submarine"), the [Barracuda class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffren-class_submarine "Suffren-class submarine"), which required converting the nuclear propulsion to conventional propulsion. Another difference was that Australia chose to equip it with a [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy") combat system and torpedo with [Lockheed Martin Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin "Lockheed Martin") selected to integrate them into the design.[[21]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuditor-General_Report202015-22)[[22]](#cite_note-23)[[23]](#cite_note-24) Australia typically requires that part of their vessels be built there, which increases the cost. In this case it corresponded to 60 per cent of the contract value, with France handling the technology transfer.[[24]](#cite_note-25)

In 2019, Australia signed a strategic partnership agreement with Naval Group to design and construct twelve submarines to be built in Australia.[[25]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuditor-General_Report20206,8,9-26)[[26]](#cite_note-27) However, the project was beset by delays and cost overruns, leading to uncertainty and tension behind the scenes.[[9]](#cite_note-recall-9)[[27]](#cite_note-Reuters22Sept-28) The revised cost, including inflation during the length of the program, was A$90 billion (€56 billion).[[28]](#cite_note-29)

In February 2021, an initial design plan was rejected as being too expensive, and Naval Group were given until September to improve their proposal.[[29]](#cite_note-paris-30) At a [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Australia "Senate of Australia") inquiry in early June 2021, with delays ongoing, Defence Secretary [Greg Moriarty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Moriarty "Greg Moriarty") revealed under questioning that he had considered making contingency plans if the French project was to fail, admitting that there had been ongoing problems[*[vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Vagueness "Wikipedia:Vagueness")*] for over a year.[[30]](#cite_note-31) Two weeks later, Australian prime minister [Scott Morrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Morrison "Scott

Morrison") met French president [Emmanuel Macron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Macron "Emmanuel Macron") in Paris and expressed concern about the project going off track, to which Macron replied that France was giving "full and complete" commitment and would proceed "further and faster if possible".[[29]](#cite_note-paris-30)

On 30 August 2021, the French and Australian defence and foreign affairs ministers released a joint statement reaffirming the project, stating that the "Ministers underlined the importance of the Future Submarine program."[[31]](#cite_note-Aug30Statement-32)[[32]](#cite_note-navalnews_2021-09-33)[[33]](#cite_note-GuardianSept18-34)

Less than three weeks later, Australia decided to publicly cancel the contract with Naval Group for the *Attack* class submarines[[16]](#cite_note-ABC-15-sep-16) despite having already spent about [A$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_dollar "Australian dollar")2.4 billion on the French project.[[34]](#cite_note-:1-35) It was expected that Australia would have to pay hundreds of millions of euros in penalties for cancelling the contract.[[35]](#cite_note-36) The contract contained "control gates" with "off-ramps" at which point Australia could withdraw from the contract.[[36]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAuditor-General_Report202028,_30-37)[[37]](#cite_note-6PR-38)

The Australian [Department of Defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Defence_(Australia) "Department of Defence (Australia)") wrote to Naval Group on the same day the security partnership was announced.[[32]](#cite_note-navalnews_2021-09-33)[[38]](#cite_note-39) The French Ministry of Defence claim the department told them that "they were satisfied with the submarine's achievable performance and with the progress of the program."[[32]](#cite_note-navalnews_2021-09-33) Naval Group said that Australia "terminated the contract for convenience".[[39]](#cite_note-40)

Morrison said that Australia now required a nuclear-powered submarine which has clear advantages of greater endurance, speed, power, stealth and carrying capacity than a conventionally-powered submarine, based on changes in the strategic situation in the Indo-Pacific.[[40]](#cite_note-bbc-41)[[41]](#cite_note-Pursuenuclear-42)[[42]](#cite_note-Morrison16thTXN-43)

### Australia–UK–US negotiations

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=AUKUS&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Australia–UK–US negotiations")]

*[The Sunday Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sunday_Telegraph "The Sunday Telegraph")* reported that in March 2021 the Australian navy chief [Vice Admiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_admiral_(Australia) "Vice admiral (Australia)") [Michael Noonan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Noonan_(admiral) "Michael Noonan (admiral)") met in London with his British counterpart [Admiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admiral_(Royal_Navy) "Admiral (Royal Navy)") [Tony Radakin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Radakin "Tony Radakin") and requested assistance from the UK and the US in acquiring nuclear-powered submarines.[[43]](#cite_note-44) *[The Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Daily_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")* reported that British Foreign Secretary [Dominic Raab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominic_Raab "Dominic Raab") "helped broker the deal".[[44]](#cite_note-Tele18Sept-45) *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* also reported that Australia first approached the UK for assistance.[[45]](#cite_note-NYT18Sept-46) *[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wall_Street_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")* reported Australia approached the US in April 2021.[[46]](#cite_note-47) A trilateral discussion was held between Johnson, Biden and Morrison at the [June 2021 G7 summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/47th_G7_summit "47th G7 summit") held in [Cornwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornwall "Cornwall"), England.[[42]](#cite_note-Morrison16thTXN-43)[[33]](#cite_note-GuardianSept18-34) The talks took place without the knowledge of the French government or Naval Group.[[44]](#cite_note-Tele18Sept-45) This approach was possible as a result of the UK not entering into a formal foreign policy and security treaty in the [post-Brexit deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EU%E2%80%93UK_Trade_and_Cooperation_Agreement "EU–UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement") with the EU. As a result, the UK was free to pursue enhanced cooperation with other allies.[[47]](#cite_note-48) [*Axios*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axios_(website) "Axios (website)") reported that the [Biden administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biden_administration "Biden administration") sought assurances from Australia that cancelling the contract was not dependent on the US providing them with assistance and that cancelling was a [fait accompli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fait_accompli "Fait accompli").[[48]](#cite_note-Axious-49) Morrison said Australia had been considering an alternative to the *Attack* class submarine deal for the past 18 months.[[42]](#cite_note-Morrison16thTXN-43)[[33]](#cite_note-GuardianSept18-34)

Although the joint announcement by Australian prime minister [Scott Morrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Morrison "Scott Morrison"), British prime minister [Boris Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson") and US president [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") did not mention any other country by name, except France, anonymous White House sources have alleged it is designed to counter the influence of Chinese forces in the [Indo-Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Pacific "Indo-Pacific") region.[[49]](#cite_note-:0-50)[[2]](#cite_note-Announce-2) However, Johnson later told parliament that the move was not intended to be "adversarial towards any other power".[[50]](#cite_note-51)

[United States secretary of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State") [Antony Blinken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antony_Blinken "Antony Blinken") and [United States secretary of defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Defense "United States Secretary of Defense") [Lloyd Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lloyd_Austin "Lloyd Austin") said that Australia did not have any "reciprocal requirements" as a consequence of the US sharing nuclear submarine propulsion technology such as Australia hosting intermediate-range missiles.[[51]](#cite_note-52)[[52]](#cite_note-dutton-dismissal-53)

### Pillar 1 – Nuclear-powered submarines

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=AUKUS&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Pillar 1 – Nuclear-powered submarines")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/President_Joe_Biden%2C_British_Prime_Minister_Rishi_Sunak_and_Australian_Prime_Minister_Anthony_Albanese_at_the_AUKUS_meeting_in_San_Diego%2C_California%2C_March_13%2C_2023_-_230313-D-TT977-0188.jpg/250px-thumbnail.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:President_Joe_Biden,_British_Prime_Minister_Rishi_Sunak_and_Australian_Prime_Minister_Anthony_Albanese_at_the_AUKUS_meeting_in_San_Diego,_California,_March_13,_2023_-_230313-D-TT977-0188.jpg)

US president [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden"), UK prime minister [Rishi Sunak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak "Rishi Sunak") and Australian prime minister [Anthony Albanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Albanese "Anthony Albanese") at the AUKUS meeting in San Diego, California, on 13 March 2023

Under the partnership, the US and UK will share nuclear propulsion technology with Australia, as they have done with each other since 1958 under the [US–UK Mutual Defence Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US%E2%80%93UK_Mutual_Defence_Agreement "US–UK Mutual Defence Agreement").[[37]](#cite_note-6PR-38)[[53]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERitchie20153,4-5-54)[[41]](#cite_note-Pursuenuclear-42) The Royal Australian Navy (RAN) will acquire at least eight nuclear-powered submarines armed with conventional weapons.[[41]](#cite_note-Pursuenuclear-42) The basic design and key technologies will be decided by the Australian [Nuclear-Powered Submarine Task Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Submarine_Agency "Australian Submarine Agency") an 18-month Department of Defence research project headed by Vice Admiral [Jonathan Mead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Mead "Jonathan Mead"), begun in September 2021 with assistance from the US and UK.[[41]](#cite_note-Pursuenuclear-42)[[54]](#cite_note-55)

Australia will extend the life of its *Collins* class submarines that the *Attack* class was due to replace and may consider leasing or buying nuclear-powered submarines from the US or the UK in the interim until the delivery of its future nuclear powered submarines.[[41]](#cite_note-Pursuenuclear-42)[[55]](#cite_note-56)[[56]](#cite_note-57) Also in the interim, Australian Defence Minister [Peter Dutton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Dutton "Peter Dutton") said that Australia will have regular visits by US and UK nuclear-powered submarines.[[57]](#cite_note-58)[[note 2]](#cite_note-60) The annual Australia-US Ministerial Consultations (AUSMIN) between the Australian Ministers for Foreign Affairs and Defence and the US Secretaries of State and Defense held in September 2021 endorsed "increasing logistics and sustainment capabilities of US surface and subsurface vessels in Australia."[[59]](#cite_note-61)[[60]](#cite_note-62)

Australia considered purchasing French nuclear submarines which use nuclear reactors fuelled by [low-enriched uranium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-enriched_uranium "Low-enriched uranium") at less than 6%.[[34]](#cite_note-:1-35)[[61]](#cite_note-princeton-63) However, French reactor designs have to be refuelled every ten years,[[34]](#cite_note-:1-35)[[62]](#cite_note-64) and Australia does not have a civil nuclear capability with [nuclear energy prohibited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_power_in_Australia "Nuclear power in Australia").[[63]](#cite_note-65) In contrast, American and British designs power the submarines for the expected life of the submarines[[34]](#cite_note-:1-35)[[64]](#cite_note-66)[[65]](#cite_note-67) using nuclear reactors fuelled by [highly enriched uranium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highly_enriched_uranium "Highly enriched uranium") (HEU) at 93% enrichment.[[66]](#cite_note-fuel-68)[[67]](#cite_note-tna3b-69)

Currently, six countries have nuclear submarines, the five permanent members of the [UN Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council") (China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States) and India.[[40]](#cite_note-bbc-41) The New York Times reported that Australia will probably buy HEU from the US for the nuclear reactor that powers the submarine.[[68]](#cite_note-70)[[note 3]](#cite_note-72) The [United States' naval reactors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_naval_reactors "United States naval reactors") are all [pressurized water reactors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressurized_water_reactor "Pressurized water reactor") (PWR).[[70]](#cite_note-73) The latest UK propulsion system is the [Rolls-Royce PWR3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolls-Royce_PWR#PWR3 "Rolls-Royce PWR") that will power the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy")'s (RN) new [*Dreadnought*-class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreadnought-class_submarine "Dreadnought-class submarine") submarines currently being built and is "based on a US design but using UK reactor technology".[[71]](#cite_note-74)[[72]](#cite_note-75)

US officials have said that sharing nuclear propulsion technology with Australia is a "one-off" and that they have no "intention of extending this to other countries".[[73]](#cite_note-76)[[74]](#cite_note-77) [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea"), also a US treaty ally, has had ambitions to acquire nuclear-powered submarines since 2017 and was reportedly refused US assistance in September 2020 because of nuclear non-proliferation.[[75]](#cite_note-78)[[76]](#cite_note-79)[[77]](#cite_note-80)

On 22 November 2021, Australia, the US and the UK signed the *Exchange of Naval Nuclear Propulsion Information Agreement* (ENNPIA) [treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty "Treaty").[[78]](#cite_note-81)[[79]](#cite_note-ENNPIA-82) The treaty permits the disclosure of information by the US and the UK to Australia and its use.[[79]](#cite_note-ENNPIA-82) The US is restricted by the [Atomic Energy Act of 1946](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_Energy_Act_of_1946 "Atomic Energy Act of 1946") from sharing information without an agreement and the UK is also restricted by the 1958 US-UK Mutual Defence Agreement unless authorised.[[80]](#cite_note-83)[[81]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERitchie20153-84) The treaty was considered in Australia by the [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Australia "Parliament of Australia")'s Joint Standing Committee on Treaties, in the UK by the [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_the_United_Kingdom "Parliament of the United Kingdom") and in the US by [Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress").[[82]](#cite_note-85)[[83]](#cite_note-86)[[84]](#cite_note-87) The ENNPIA treaty entered into force on 8 February 2022.[[5]](#cite_note-FactSheet-5)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/One_of_the_first_RAN_graduates_of_the_USN_Nuclear_Power_School_with_dignitaries_during_their_graduation_ceremony_in_July_2023.jpg/250px-One_of_the_first_RAN_graduates_of_the_USN_Nuclear_Power_School_with_dignitaries_during_their_graduation_ceremony_in_July_2023.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:One_of_the_first_RAN_graduates_of_the_USN_Nuclear_Power_School_with_dignitaries_during_their_graduation_ceremony_in_July_2023.jpg)

One of the first three Royal Australian Navy officers to graduate from the US Navy's [Nuclear Power School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_Power_School "Nuclear Power School") posing with Australian and American dignitaries in July 2023

On 31 August 2022, the UK announced that Australian submariners would receive training aboard [*Astute*-class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astute-class_submarine "Astute-class submarine") [submarines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine "Submarine").[[85]](#cite_note-88)

On 13 March 2023, AUKUS announced that a new nuclear powered submarine class would be built in the UK and Australia to be called the [SSN-AUKUS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SSN-AUKUS "SSN-AUKUS"), also known as the SSN-A.[[86]](#cite_note-89)[[87]](#cite_note-90)[[88]](#cite_note-AUKUSMar23-91) The US intends to sell Australia three nuclear-powered [*Virginia* class](https://en

.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia-class_submarine "Virginia-class submarine") submarines, subject to [congressional approval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress"), to ensure there is no capability gap as the *Collins* class submarines are retired, with the potential to sell up to two more if needed.[[1]](#cite_note-:8-1)[[89]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMinistry_of_Defence202310-92) RAN personnel will be embedded in the RN and USN to receive nuclear training and at UK and US submarine industrial bases.[[88]](#cite_note-AUKUSMar23-91) The Submarine Rotational Force-West initiative which will from as early as 2027 base USN *Virginia* class and RN *Astute* class submarines on a rotational basis at the RAN's HMAS *Stirling* submarine base in order to accelerate Australia's ability to operate nuclear-powered submarines and to contribute to security in the Indo-Pacific region.[[90]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMinistry_of_Defence20238,_27,_29-93)

The SSN-AUKUS class will based on the UK SSNR design already under development.[[91]](#cite_note-94)[[92]](#cite_note-95) The RN is planned to receive its first SSN-AUKUS class submarine as early as the late 2030s.[[93]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMinistry_of_Defence20237-96) The RAN is planned to receive their first submarine in the early 2040s.[[93]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMinistry_of_Defence20237-96) Australia will reportedly build five SSN-AUKUS submarines.[[94]](#cite_note-97) The RAN is planned to receive their first *Virginia* class submarine from the US in the early 2030s.[[95]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMinistry_of_Defence20238-98)

The [Australian Submarine Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Submarine_Agency "Australian Submarine Agency") was established on 1 July 2023. It has the role of managing the Australian nuclear submarine program, and includes personnel posted to the UK and US.[[96]](#cite_note-99)

In November 2023, Capt. Lincoln Reifsteck USN, the USN's AUKUS integration and acquisition program manager, talked at the Naval Submarine League's annual symposium. He said that, in 2032 and 2035, the US will sell to Australia in-service Block IV *Virginia* class submarines, the first of which was commissioned in 2020, and the final will likely commission around 2026. Thus, Australia would receive submarines with between six and 15 years' worth of use, out of their designed service life of 33 years. He also said that the US would sell a new Block VII boat to Australia in 2038, the Block VIIs being the original *Virginia* class length without the Virginia Payload Module, set to begin construction in FY2029.[[97]](#cite_note-100)

In August 2024, Australian prime minister [Anthony Albanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Albanese "Anthony Albanese"), made undisclosed "political commitments" with its AUKUS partners in an agreement for the transfer of naval nuclear technology to Australia, sparking concerns about the potential for high-level radioactive waste to be stored in the country. The White House confirmed that Australia, the UK, and the US reached a significant milestone in their cooperation, essential for Australia's future nuclear-powered submarine capabilities. Despite assurances from the government, critics, including the [Greens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Greens "Australian Greens"), warned of possible loopholes that could lead to uranium enrichment and radioactive waste management in Australia.[[98]](#cite_note-101)

On 1 June 2025, the UK government announced that it will build up to twelve SSN-AUKUS submarines to replace the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy")'s seven [*Astute-*class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astute-class_submarine "Astute-class submarine") attack submarines from the late 2030s. The announcement also said that there will be a major expansion of industrial capability at [BAE Systems Submarines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAE_Systems_Submarines "BAE Systems Submarines") at [Barrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrow-in-Furness "Barrow-in-Furness") and at [Rolls-Royce Submarines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolls-Royce_Submarines "Rolls-Royce Submarines") at [Derby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby "Derby"), with a new boat scheduled to be built every eighteen months.[[99]](#cite_note-102)[[100]](#cite_note-103) On 26 July 2025, the UK and Australian governments signed the **Geelong Treaty**, a 50-year bilateral defence agreement to facilitate bilateral cooperation on the construction of Australia's SSN-AUKUS submarines.[[101]](#cite_note-104)

On 30 May 2026, at an AUKUS Defence Minister's Meeting held in Singapore it was announced that the third *Virginia-*class boat that Australia is planned to receive will now be an in-service Block IV boat the same as the first two. This will simplify fleet training and maintenance for Australia and save them significant costs.[[102]](#cite_note-105)[[103]](#cite_note-:6-106)

### Pillar 2 – Advanced Capabilities

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=AUKUS&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Pillar 2 – Advanced Capabilities")]

AUKUS Pillar 2 encompasses a wide array of activities (including many commonly referred to by the US Department of Defense as international armaments cooperation). There may include information and personnel exchange, cooperative research, development, testing, and evaluation, and joint production. In contrast to Pillar 1 activities, which will take decades to deliver results, Pillar 2 is likely to produce more immediate capability improvements.[[104]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENicastro20244-107)

#### Undersea Capabilities

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=AUKUS&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Undersea Capabilities")]

Undersea capabilities, in the context of AUKUS, refer to systems and technologies that operate underwater but are not crewed submarines.[[105]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENicastro20245-108) Pillar 2 activities in this area include the “AUKUS Maritime Autonomy Experimentation and Exercise Series,” which the three governments have described as “a series of integrated trilateral experiments and exercises aimed at enhancing capability development, improving interoperability, and increasing the sophistication and scale of autonomous systems in the maritime domain.”[[106]](#cite_note-:5-109) The AUKUS governments are also working on the ability to deploy and recover UUVs (Uncrewed Underwater Vehicles) from crewed submarines (sometimes referred to as “launch and recovery”), conducting activities to develop and improve “the ability to launch and recover undersea vehicles from torpedo tubes on current classes of submarines to deliver effects such as strike and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance.”[[106]](#cite_note-:5-109) In November 2023, the United States Department of Defense announced that the AUKUS partners had participated in a joint exercise to demonstrate and improve capabilities relating to the protection of underwater infrastructure and the use of autonomous and semiautonomous undersea systems.[[107]](#cite_note-110)

The Defence Minister's meeting on 30 May 2026 announced that the first signature project of Pillar 2 would be cutting-edge sensors, payloads and weapons systems for UUVs with delivery to commence in 2027.[[103]](#cite_note-:6-106)[[108]](#cite_note-111)

#### Quantum Technologies

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=AUKUS&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Quantum Technologies")]

As part of the Quantum Technologies working group, the AUKUS nations have established the AUKUS Quantum Arrangement (AQuA), an initiative to coordinate U.S., British, and Australian RDT&E efforts concerning quantum technologies. Initial AQuA efforts were expected to focus on developing alternate solutions for position, navigation, and timing (similar to current Global Positioning System capability) through trials and experimentation through 2025.[[109]](#cite_note-112) Additionally, the AUKUS governments announced in December 2023 that they were “accelerating the development of quantum technologies for positioning, navigation, and timing in military capabilities,” with a particular focus on improving “resilience for our trilateral forces in Global Positioning System-degraded environments and enhance stealth in the undersea domain.”[[106]](#cite_note-:5-109)

The announcement of AUKUS included the stated aim of improving "joint capabilities and interoperability. These initial efforts will focus on cyber capabilities, artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, and additional undersea capabilities."[[110]](#cite_note-113) [Tom Tugendhat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Tugendhat "Tom Tugendhat"), chair of the [British Commons' Foreign Affairs Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Affairs_Select_Committee "Foreign Affairs Select Committee"), later commented on Twitter that "Bringing together the military-industrial complex of these three allies together is a step-change in the relationship. We've always been interoperable, but this aims at much more. From [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") to advanced technology the US, UK and Australia will now be able to cost save by increasing platform sharing and innovation costs. Particularly for the smaller two, that's game-changing."[[111]](#cite_note-et-114) *Engineering & Technology* pointed to the increasing expansion of Chinese technology firms such as [Huawei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huawei "Huawei"), which has been excluded from tendering for participation in telecommunications networks by the US and Australia on national security grounds, and government vetoes over the attempted Chinese acquisition of American company [Lattice Semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_Semiconductor "Lattice Semiconductor") and ongoing British consideration of proposed takeovers of local semiconductor firms.[[111]](#cite_note-et-114) *Engineering & Technology* also pointed to the March 2021 statement of the US National Security Commission on AI, of the imperative to intensify local efforts but also "rally our closest allies and partners to defend and compete in the coming era of AI-accelerated competition and conflict".[[111]](#cite_note-et-114)

#### Hypersonic and Counter-Hypersonic Capabilities

On January 19, 2023, the [United States](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") hit its [debt ceiling](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_debt_ceiling "United States debt ceiling"), leading to a debt-ceiling crisis, part of an ongoing political debate within [Congress](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") about [federal government spending](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_federal_budget "United States federal budget") and the [national debt](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_debt_of_the_United_States "National debt of the United States") that the U.S. government accrues.[[1]](#cite_note-Bloomberg.com-1)[[2]](#cite_note-nbcpalmsprings.com-2) In response, [U.S. treasury secretary](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_the_Treasury "United States Secretary of the Treasury") [Janet Yellen](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janet_Yellen "Janet Yellen") began enacting temporary "extraordinary measures". On May 1, 2023, Yellen warned these measures could be exhausted as early as June 1, 2023;[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) this date was later pushed to June 5.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

The debt ceiling had been increased multiple times through December 2021 since the [2013 debt-ceiling standoff](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_United_States_debt-ceiling_crisis "2013 United States debt-ceiling crisis"), each time without budgetary preconditions attached.[[6]](#cite_note-:3-6)[[7]](#cite_note-PIonline-7) In the 2023 impasse, Republicans proposed cutting spending back to 2022 levels as a precondition to raising the debt ceiling, while Democrats insisted on a "clean bill" without preconditions, as had been the case in raising the ceiling 3 times during the [first Donald Trump administration](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump").[[8]](#cite_note-Snopes-8)

If the government had run out of funds, the Treasury would have had to either default on payments to bondholders or immediately curtail payment of funds owed to various companies and individuals that had been mandated but not fully funded by Congress. Both situations had been expected to result in a global economic meltdown.[[9]](#cite_note-9) Additionally, if the federal government had been unable to issue new debt, it would have had to balance its budget by imposing budget cuts that, in total, would have equaled 5% of the size of the American economy.[[10]](#cite_note-10) Constitutional scholar [Laurence Tribe](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_Tribe "Laurence Tribe") said that a default would be unconstitutional due to the [14th Amendment](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution") and the government would be required to repay its debts despite hitting the debt ceiling.[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-12) President [Joe Biden](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") said that he was considering invoking the 14th Amendment because he felt he had authority to do so, but questioned whether it could be done in time to avoid default given the possibility that it might be appealed.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

#### Federal budget and deficit

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2023_United_States_debt-ceiling_crisis&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Federal budget and deficit")]

In 2019, just over 60% of the [federal budget](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_federal_budget "United States federal budget") went to mandatory spending for programs like Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid, with another 30% going to discretionary spending (half of which went to defense). The remaining 9% went to pay for interest on the debt. Meanwhile, both mandatory spending programs and interest on the debt were expected to take up increasing shares of the federal budget, while tax revenues were expected to be stagnant.[[17]](#cite_note-:10-17)

In addition, it has run deficits every year since 2001, when it last ran a surplus.[[18]](#cite_note-18) Financing a deficit requires that the government borrow money.[[19]](#cite_note-19)

However, based on [Article 1](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Article_One_of_the_United_States_Constitution "Article One of the United States Constitution"), Section 8, Clause 2 of the [United States Constitution](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_United_States "Constitution of the United States"), only Congress has the authority to borrow money "on the Credit of the United States".[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21)[[22]](#cite_note-22)

In 1939, Congress gave the treasury the right to issue and manage debt—though it limited how much it could issue. From 1939 to 2018, the treasury increased the debt ceiling 98 times, decreasing it five times.[[25]](#cite_note-25) Whilst the treasury can borrow money to pay for federal expenditures, it is limited in power by Congress.[[26]](#cite_note-auto-26)

In other words, the treasury can borrow money to pay for federal expenditures—but only as much as Congress lets it.[[26]](#cite_note-auto-26)

Since 2009, America's [national debt](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_debt_of_the_United_States "National debt of the United States") has nearly tripled, with annual federal deficits averaging close to $1 trillion since 2001.[[27]](#cite_note-:8-27) During the 21st century, it has gone up for various reasons, including tax cuts under presidents [Bush](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bush_tax_cuts "Bush tax cuts") and [Trump](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_Cuts_and_Jobs_Act_of_2017 "Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017"), wars in [Iraq](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War "Iraq War") and [Afghanistan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Afghanistan_(2001–2021) "War in Afghanistan (2001–2021)"), entitlements like [Medicare Part D](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_Part_D "Medicare Part D"), and spending in response to the [Great Recession](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Recession_in_the_United_States "Great Recession in the United States") and the [COVID-19 pandemic](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"). Currently, the U.S. is the industrialized country with the fourth highest debt-to-GDP ratio, behind Japan, Italy and Greece. Additionally, the national debt is forecast to be double the United States' GDP by 2051.[[17]](#cite_note-:10-17)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2023_United_States_debt-ceiling_crisis&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Reducing the deficit and debt")]

According to both policy experts and politicians, dealing with the deficit and debt will ultimately involve both raising taxes and decreasing spending. However, it tends to be difficult to do so in practice, owing to citizens' reluctance to alter large programs like Social Security or the raising of taxes. Historically, no political party has been willing to reduce the deficit or debt when they have held power, although the issue is often a foundation of candidates' election campaigns.[[28]](#cite_note-28)

The [United States debt ceiling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_debt_ceiling "United States debt ceiling") is a legislative limit that determines how much debt the Treasury Department may incur.[[23]](#cite_note-bbc-20211015-23) It was introduced in 1917, when Congress voted to give Treasury the right to issue bonds for financing America participating in World War I,[[24]](#cite_note-24) rather than issuing them for individual projects, as had been the case in the past. In 1939, Congress gave the treasury the right to issue and manage debt—though it limited how much it could issue. From 1939 to 2018, the treasury increased the debt ceiling 98 times, decreasing it five times.[[25]](#cite_note-25) Whilst the treasury can borrow money to pay for federal expenditures, it is limited in power by Congress.[[26]](#cite_note-auto-26)

In other words, the treasury can borrow money to pay for federal expenditures—but only as much as Congress lets it.[[26]](#cite_note-auto-26)

Since 2009, America's [national debt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_debt_of_the_United_States "National debt of the United States") has nearly tripled, with annual federal deficits averaging close to $1 trillion since 2001.[[27]](#cite_note-:8-27) During the 21st century, it has gone up for various reasons, including tax cuts under presidents [Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bush_tax_cuts "Bush tax cuts") and [Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_Cuts_and_Jobs_Act_of_2017 "Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017"), wars in [Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War "Iraq War") and [Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Afghanistan_(2001%E2%80%932021) "War in Afghanistan (2001–2021)"), entitlements like [Medicare Part D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_Part_D "Medicare Part D"), and spending in response to the [Great Recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Recession_in_the_United_States "Great Recession in the United States") and the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"). Currently, the U.S. is the industrialized country with the fourth highest debt-to-GDP ratio, behind Japan, Italy and Greece. Additionally, the national debt is forecast to be double the United States' GDP by 2051.[[17]](#cite_note-:10-17)

#### Reducing the deficit and debt

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2023_United_States_debt-ceiling_crisis&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Reducing the deficit and debt")]

According to both policy experts and politicians, dealing with the deficit and debt will ultimately involve both raising taxes and decreasing spending. Past plans for taxes hikes have included reducing the number of deductions, increasing rates on higher earners, and making new taxes, while proposals for reducing spending have included reducing Social Security benefits, lowering payments for Medicaid and Medicare, and cutting defense spending, among others.[[17]](#cite_note-:10-17)

However, it tends to be difficult to do so in practice, owing to citizens' reluctance to alter large programs like Social Security or the raising of taxes. Historically, no political party has been willing to reduce the deficit or debt when they have held power, although the issue is often a foundation of candidates' election campaigns.[[28]](#cite_note-28)

### The U.S. dollar and borrowing

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2023_United_States_debt-ceiling_crisis&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: The U.S. dollar and borrowing")]

The [United States dollar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar") (used heavily in international trade) is considered to be the world's reserve currency for a variety of reasons including the sheer magnitude of the American economy, America's geopolitical strength, the dollar's relative stability, and the market for U.S. debt.[[29]](#cite_note-29)

As well, the [Compromise of 1790](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compromise_of_1790 "Compromise of 1790") (when Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton got both Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson and Representative James Madison to agree to take on Revolutionary War debts assumed by the states and the Continental Congress in exchange for locating the capital on the Potomac River by Virginia[[30]](#cite_note-30)) played a role with this: Because Revolutionary War bondholders were paid 100 cents on the dollar, America made good on its debt and established good credit. This, in turn, helped contribute to the dollar becoming the world's reserve currency.[[31]](#cite_note-:15-31)

As a result, foreign creditors (including China, Japan, and the United Kingdom) are large markets for the currency. This makes it easier for the U.S. government to finance the national debt via being charged lower interest rates for borrowing money.[[17]](#cite_note-:10-17)

|  |  |

|  | Parts of this article (those related to the Trump administration's support for Israel) need to be **updated**. Please help update this article to reflect recent events or newly available information. *(May 2025)* |

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/P20231009AS-0695_%2853248442634%29.jpg/250px-P20231009AS-0695_%2853248442634%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:P20231009AS-0695_(53248442634).jpg)

The [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") illuminated in the colors of the [Israeli flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_flag "Israeli flag") on 9 October 2023




The [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") has provided extensive military, diplomatic, and financial support to [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel") during the [Gaza war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war "Gaza war"). This included rapid deployment of warships and military aircraft, billions in military aid and expedited weapons shipments —including [guided missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guided_missiles "Guided missiles"), [artillery shells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artillery_shells "Artillery shells"), and advanced defense systems.

After an initial period of [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_world "Western world") support for Israel's offensive, Israel and the United States became increasingly isolated amid growing worldwide [calls for a ceasefire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calls_for_a_ceasefire_during_the_Gaza_war "Calls for a ceasefire during the Gaza war"),[[1]](#cite_note-Time-2023-1)[[2]](#cite_note-AP_News-2023-2)[[3]](#cite_note-The_Guardian-2023-3) with the US vetoing three [United Nations Security Council resolutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_resolution "United Nations Security Council resolution") calling for a humanitarian ceasefire.[[4]](#cite_note-NBC_News-2023-4) International rights groups have condemned the U.S. for providing support to Israel that they say risks complicity in [Israeli war crimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_war_crimes_in_the_Gaza_war "Israeli war crimes in the Gaza war") and violations of the [Leahy Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leahy_Law "Leahy Law") and [Foreign Assistance Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Assistance_Act_of_1974 "Foreign Assistance Act of 1974"), although the latter was officially rejected by the [U.S. Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate "U.S. Senate").[[5]](#cite_note-Lederer-2023-5)[[6]](#cite_note-Ratcliffe-2023-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7)

As the war went on, tensions between the Israeli government and the [Biden administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biden_administration "Biden administration") began to grow.[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9) The US government became more publicly critical of Israel as Palestinian civilian [casualties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casualties_of_the_Gaza_war "Casualties of the Gaza war") rose and opposition grew. Over a dozen U.S. officials resigned and there were large-scale demonstrations on university campuses and outside defense contractors. In February 2024, the Biden administration issued a [national security directive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_security_directive "National security directive") requiring written assurances from Israel that it was using US-supplied weapons in line with international law. In March 2024, the US began calling for an immediate and sustained ceasefire linked to the release of hostages, and Israel criticized the US for allowing [a ceasefire resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_2728 "United Nations Security Council Resolution 2728") to pass at the [UN Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UN_Security_Council "UN Security Council"). The US also voiced its opposition to much of Israel's post-war plan for Gaza.[[10]](#cite_note-10) Despite this, however, American weapons transfers to Israel continued.[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-12)

## Background

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Total_US_foreign_assistance_by_country%2C_adjusted_for_inflation%2C_1946-2022.png/330px-Total_US_foreign_assistance_by_country%2C_adjusted_for_inflation%2C_1946-2022.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Total_US_foreign_assistance_by_country,_adjusted_for_inflation,_1946-2022.png)

Graph showing recipients of [U.S. foreign aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_foreign_aid "United States foreign aid"), 1946–2022[[13]](#cite_note-13)

After Hamas-led Palestinian armed groups attacked Israel on 7 October, resulting in the death of 1,195 Israelis, 828 of which were civilians, Israel began a campaign against Gaza.[[14]](#cite_note-Holland-2023-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16)
Since the start of the Israeli operation, more than 73,000 Palestinians in Gaza have been killed, of whom almost half of identified were [women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_Gaza_war "Women in the Gaza war") and [children](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effect_of_the_Gaza_war_on_children_in_the_Gaza_Strip "Effect of the Gaza war on children in the Gaza Strip").[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18)[[19]](#cite_note-19) Almost 8,000 Palestinians are missing and presumed trapped under rubble.[[20]](#cite_note-20) Israel placed Gaza under a [complete blockade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_blockade_of_the_Gaza_Strip_(2023%E2%80%93present) "Israeli blockade of the Gaza Strip (2023–present)"), including the prevention of fuel and water from entering the Gaza Strip.[[21]](#cite_note-Harb-2023-21)[[22]](#cite_note-22)[[23]](#cite_note-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24)[[25]](#cite_note-25) The United States described Hamas-led attack as "unprovoked,"[[26]](#cite_note-26) and started sending warships and warplanes into the region, prepared to give Israel whatever it needs.[[27]](#cite_note-Copp-2023-27) Civil rights groups such as the [Center for Constitutional Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Constitutional_Rights "Center for Constitutional Rights") meanwhile called on the government to address the underlying issues that have led to the recent violence, such as Israel's illegal [possession of the Palestinian lands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli-occupied_territories "Israeli-occupied territories") and its [blockade of Gaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockade_of_the_Gaza_Strip "Blockade of the Gaza Strip") as well as "the [apartheid regime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_and_apartheid "Israel and apartheid") throughout historic Palestine".[[28]](#cite_note-Speri-2023-28)

Following Israel's victory over surrounding Arab forces in the [1967 Six-Day War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six-Day_War "Six-Day War") and its subsequent occupation of the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Gaza, military assistance to the country surged significantly. The [Iron Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Dome "Iron Dome"), which became operational in 2011, was created with the help of the United States, which is responsible for providing components for the system, including allocating more than $1.5 billion for missile defense for Israel in 2022.[[29]](#cite_note-How_big_is_Israel-2023-29)
As part of a record $38 billion agreement over ten years negotiated under former US President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") in 2016, US military aid to Israel exceeded $3.8 billion in 2023. Of this $3.8 billion, half a billion was for Israel's missile defense. Washington has announced that it will replenish Israel's ammunition used in the war.[[29]](#cite_note-How_big_is_Israel-2023-29)

## Military support

### Weapons transfers

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/U_S_Air_Force_Airmen_supply_Israel_with_missile_defense_%288086168%29.jpg/250px-U_S_Air_Force_Airmen_supply_Israel_with_missile_defense_%288086168%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:U_S_Air_Force_Airmen_supply_Israel_with_missile_defense_(8086168).jpg)

[USAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USAF "USAF") airmen prepare for departure in a [C-17 Globemaster III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C-17_Globemaster_III "C-17 Globemaster III") carrying ammunition to Israel, 15 October 2023, at [Ramstein Air Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramstein_Air_Base "Ramstein Air Base"), Germany.

The Biden administration caused controversy after bypassing Congress on multiple occasions to authorize arms sales to the Israeli military.[[30]](#cite_note-30) Unlike the [United States' military support for Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_and_the_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "United States and the Russian invasion of Ukraine"), details of weapons sent to Israel have been vague.[[31]](#cite_note-31) Leaked details have shown that the U.S. has sent [laser-guided missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser-guided_bomb "Laser-guided bomb"), [155mm shells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/155_mm_caliber "155 mm caliber"), new army vehicles, among others, at Israel's request.[[32]](#cite_note-32) According to the [Costs of War Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costs_of_War_Project "Costs of War Project") at [Brown University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_University "Brown University"), the United States spent $21.7 billion on military aid to Israel from October 2023 to September 2025.[[33]](#cite_note-33)[[34]](#cite_note-34)

In December 2023, the WSJ report stated that US arms shipments to Israel since the start of the war included 15,000 bombs and 57,000 [155mm artillery shells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/155_mm_caliber "155 mm caliber"). The United States also delivered 100 [BLU-109](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BLU-109_bomb "BLU-109 bomb") [bunker buster bombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunker_buster "Bunker buster"), 5,000 unguided [Mk82 bombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_82_bomb "Mark 82 bomb"), more than 5,400 [Mk84 bombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_84_bomb "Mark 84 bomb"), about 1,000 small diameter [GBU-39 bombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GBU-39_Small_Diameter_Bomb "GBU-39 Small Diameter Bomb"), and approximately 3,000 [JDAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Direct_Attack_Munition "Joint Direct Attack Munition") guidance kits.[[35]](#cite_note-US_sends-2023-35)

An investigation by *[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")* found the U.S. government was using special mechanisms to protect Israel from domestic human rights laws to continue sending weapons.[[36]](#cite_note-36) Following a trip to Washington D.C. in June 2024, Israeli defense minister [Yoav Gallant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoav_Gallant "Yoav Gallant") addressed Israeli complaints about slowed arms transfers, stating, "Obstacles were removed and bottlenecks were addressed".[[37]](#cite_note-37) A report by [ProPublica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ProPublica "ProPublica") found the U.S. State Department had ignored reports about potential human rights violations by the Israeli army to continue weapons transfers to Israel.[[38]](#cite_note-38) Current and former State Department officials stated there were more than 500 reports of Israel using U.S. weapons to cause "unnecessary harm to civilians" in the Gaza Strip, but that no action had yet been taken on any of the reports.[[39]](#cite_note-39)

Unnamed officials stated in March 2024 that the U.S. had signed off on an additional 1,800 [MK84](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_84_bomb "Mark 84 bomb") 2,000-pound bombs and 500 [MK82](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_82_bomb "Mark 82 bomb") 500-pound bombs.[[40]](#cite_note-40) In May 2024, Israel used two U.S.-made [GBU-39](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GBU-39_Small_Diameter_Bomb "GBU-39 Small Diameter Bomb") missiles during the [Tel al-Sultan massacre](https://en.wikip
