Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Title_42_expulsion:
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/2020-_Title_42_expulsions_-_southwest_U.S._border.svg/330px-2020-_Title_42_expulsions_-_southwest_U.S._border.svg.png)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2020-_Title_42_expulsions_-_southwest_U.S._border.svg)

Section 362 of the Public Health Service Act ([42 U.S.C.](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Title_42_of_the_United_States_Code "Title 42 of the United States Code") [§ 265](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/265))[[1]](#cite_note-42usc265_text-1) governs suspension of entries to prevent spread of communicable diseases. Shown: expulsions from the southwest U.S. border at the time of the [COVID-19 pandemic](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic").[[2]](#cite_note-2)

A **Title 42 expulsion** is the [removal](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deportation_and_removal_from_the_United_States "Deportation and removal from the United States"), out of the territory of the United States, by the U.S. government, of a person who has recently been in a country where a [communicable disease](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communicable_disease "Communicable disease") was present. The extent of authority for such contagion-related expulsions is set out in federal law in section 362 of the [Public Health Service Act of 1944](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Health_Service_Act "Public Health Service Act") ([42 U.S.C.](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Title_42_of_the_United_States_Code "Title 42 of the United States Code") [§ 265](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/265)).

During the [COVID-19 pandemic](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), the [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention") (CDC) under the [Trump administration](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump"), used this provision to generally block land entry for many migrants. This practice was initially continued by the [Biden administration](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biden_administration "Biden administration")[[3]](#cite_note-Title_42_with_expansion-3) but was halted with the end of the [COVID-19 national emergency](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Emergency_Concerning_the_Southern_Border_of_the_United_States "National Emergency Concerning the Southern Border of the United States"), on May 12, 2023. [Title 42 of the United States Code](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Title_42_of_the_United_States_Code "Title 42 of the United States Code") includes numerous sections dealing with [public health](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_health "Public health"), [social welfare](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_welfare "Social welfare"), and [civil rights](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights "Civil rights"), but, in the context of [immigration](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration "Immigration"), the phrase "Title 42" came to be used to refer specifically to expulsions under section 362.

The program allows [U.S. Customs and Border Protection](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Customs_and_Border_Protection "U.S. Customs and Border Protection") (CBP) to prohibit the entry of persons who potentially pose a health risk by being subject to previously announced travel restrictions or by unlawfully entering the country to bypass health-screening measures.[[4]](#cite_note-Title42-FY2021-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Title42-FY2020-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) Persons subject to the order are not held in congregate areas for processing and are instead immediately expelled to their country of last transit.[[5]](#cite_note-Title42-FY2020-5) If they are unable to be returned to the country of last transit (because that country will not accept them due to their nationality), CBP will work with its interagency partners to expel the person to their country of origin.[[5]](#cite_note-Title42-FY2020-5) In some cases, this is not possible, and migrants may be expelled to a third country that will accept them based on previous residency.[[7]](#cite_note-7) Expulsions under Title 42 are not based on immigration status and are tracked separately from immigration.[[5]](#cite_note-Title42-FY2020-5) At the discretion of the presidential administration, Title 42 can be used even for people who would normally have [temporary protected status](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temporary_protected_status "Temporary protected status") based on their country of origin.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

The CDC's policy under Title 42 was unenforceable from November 15, 2022, when D.C. federal judge [Emmet G. Sullivan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmet_G._Sullivan "Emmet G. Sullivan") ruled that the policy is a violation of the [Administrative Procedure Act](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrative_Procedure_Act_(United_States) "Administrative Procedure Act (United States)"),[[9]](#cite_note-Alvarez-9) until December 19 when the [chief justice of the United States](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_justice_of_the_United_States "Chief justice of the United States"), [John Roberts](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Roberts "John Roberts"), issued a temporary hold on Sullivan's ruling,[[10]](#cite_note-SCOTUS_22A544-10) followed by the full court in a 5–4 vote on December 27.[[11]](#cite_note-Stohr-11)

In the days preceding the policy's repeal on May 11, 2023, the number of migrants crossing the border increased.[[12]](#cite_note-:2-12) To mitigate the potential surge in border crossings following the end of Title 42, the federal government implemented new rules for incoming migrants at the US-Mexico border. These new rules bar from the United States those who attempt to enter illegally for five years if they do not qualify for asylum.[[12]](#cite_note-:2-12) The new rule also presumes that migrants are ineligible for asylum if they did not arrive at a legal port of entry or if they passed through other countries first without seeking asylum.[[12]](#cite_note-:2-12) This policy has contributed to a decline in both 'gotaways' and border encounters as those who are apprehended are subject to stricter rules upon removal from the United States if they were to attempt to reenter.

Section 362 of the [Public Health Service Act of 1944](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Health_Service_Act "Public Health Service Act") ([42 U.S.C.](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Title_42_of_the_United_States_Code "Title 42 of the United States Code") [§ 265](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/265)), the statutory authority in question, reads as follows:[[13]](#cite_note-:0-13)

:   **§362. Suspension of entries and imports from designated places to prevent spread of communicable diseases**

    :   Whenever the Surgeon General determines that by reason of the existence of any communicable disease in a foreign country there is serious danger of the introduction of such disease into the United States, and that this danger is so increased by the introduction of persons or property from such country that a suspension of the right to introduce such persons and property is required in the interest of the public health, the Surgeon General, in accordance with regulations approved by the President, shall have the power to prohibit, in whole or in part, the introduction of persons and property from such countries or places as he shall designate in order to avert such danger, and for such period of time as he may deem necessary for such purpose.

In March 2020, the Center for Disease Control under the [Trump administration](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump") issued a public health order allowing for the rapid expulsion of unauthorized border crossers and asylum seekers, citing [COVID-19](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19") concerns.[[14]](#cite_note-14) As it is considered an "expulsion" rather than a "deportation", the migrants were not afforded the right to make a case to stay in the U.S. before an immigration judge.[[15]](#cite_note-15) Most migrants subject to the orders were returned to Mexico within hours.[[16]](#cite_note-BarrOwen-16) Trump advisor [Stephen Miller](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Miller_(political_advisor) "Stephen Miller (political advisor)") had a role in shaping the policy,[[17]](#cite_note-17) and has since defended it in interviews.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

In November 2020, a federal court ordered a halt to the practice in regard to unaccompanied minor children;[[19]](#cite_note-19) on January 29, 2021, the stay was lifted by [DC Circuit Court of Appeals](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Circuit_Court_of_Appeals "DC Circuit Court of Appeals"), allowing minors to be expelled pending its review of the case.[[20]](#cite_note-20)

In February 2021, Mexico stopped accepting families with children under the program.[[16]](#cite_note-BarrOwen-16) [Physicians for Human Rights](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physicians_for_Human_Rights "Physicians for Human Rights") noted that the policy had been applied unfairly against migrants and asylees and that its stated purpose of containing the spread of [COVID-19](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19") was dubious as the U.S. continued to allow millions of people to cross the [US–Mexico border](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico–United_States_border "Mexico–United States border") weekly.[[21]](#cite_note-21)[[22]](#cite_note-BCdata2021-22)[[23]](#cite_note-23) In early February 2021, the Mexican government announced that it would stop accepting non-Mexican family units with minor children returned to Mexico under Title 42.[[24]](#cite_note-24)[[25]](#cite_note-25)

In June 2021, it was reported that the Biden administration had been considering rescinding Title 42.[[26]](#cite_note-26) However, in September 2021, [NPR](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR") reported that the administration had defended Title 42 expulsion in court under the pretext of slowing the spread of COVID-19.[[27]](#cite_note-27)

The **Inflation Reduction Act of 2022** (**IRA**), [Pub. L.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Act_of_Congress#Public_law,_private_law,_designation "Act of Congress") [117–169 (text)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/117/public/169?link-type=html) [(PDF)](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/117/public/169?link-type=pdf&.pdf), is a [United States federal law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_the_United_States "Law of the United States") which aimed to [reduce the federal government budget deficit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deficit_reduction_in_the_United_States "Deficit reduction in the United States"), lower [prescription drug prices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prescription_drug_prices_in_the_United_States "Prescription drug prices in the United States"), and invest in domestic energy production while promoting [renewable energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renewable_energy "Renewable energy"). It was passed by the [117th United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/117th_United_States_Congress "117th United States Congress") and signed into law by President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") on August 16, 2022.

It is a [budget reconciliation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconciliation_(United_States_Congress) "Reconciliation (United States Congress)") bill sponsored by senators [Chuck Schumer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Schumer "Chuck Schumer") ([D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)")-[NY](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)")) and [Joe Manchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Manchin "Joe Manchin") (D-[WV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Virginia "West Virginia")).[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) The bill was the result of negotiations on the proposed [Build Back Better Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Build_Back_Better_Act "Build Back Better Act"), which was reduced and comprehensively reworked from its initial proposal after being opposed by Manchin.[[2]](#cite_note-2) It was introduced as an amendment to the Build Back Better Act and the legislative text was substituted. All Democrats in the Senate and House voted for the bill while all voting Republicans voted against it.[[3]](#cite_note-:10-3)[[4]](#cite_note-:11-4) It was described as a landmark piece of legislation.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)

According to the nonpartisan [Congressional Budget Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Budget_Office "Congressional Budget Office") (CBO) and [Joint Committee on Taxation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congressional_Joint_Committee_on_Taxation "United States Congressional Joint Committee on Taxation") (JCT), the law will raise $738 billion from [tax reform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_reform "Tax reform") and prescription drug reform to lower prices, as well as authorize $891 billion in total spending – including $391 billion on [energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_in_the_United_States "Energy in the United States") and [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change_in_the_United_States "Climate change in the United States"), and 64 billion on three years of [Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act") subsidies.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)[[7]](#cite_note-:7-7) It represents the largest investment towards addressing [greenhouse gas emissions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenhouse_gas_emissions "Greenhouse gas emissions") in United States history.[[8]](#cite_note-8) It also includes a large expansion of the [Internal Revenue Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_Revenue_Service "Internal Revenue Service") (IRS), including the hiring of up to 87,000 new employees to replace tens of thousands of recent departures, which led to over $1 billion being collected in past-due taxes from [millionaires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millionaire "Millionaire") and other high-wealth individuals by July 2024.[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[a]](#cite_note-11)

The act is generally not believed to have reduced [inflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation "Inflation") in 2022 and 2023,[[11]](#cite_note-12)[[12]](#cite_note-13) although some economists predict the renewable energy investments will bring down inflation in the medium-to-long term.[[13]](#cite_note-:14-14)[[14]](#cite_note-:4-15)

In 2026, the first group of 10 high-cost drugs selected by Medicare will have their negotiated prices take effect.[[15]](#cite_note-WordBrown2022-16)

The Build Back Better Plan was a legislative framework proposed by United States president [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") between 2020 and 2021. Generally viewed as ambitious in size and scope, it sought to make the largest nationwide public investments in social, infrastructural, and environmental programs since the 1930s [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression")-fighting policies of the [New Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal "New Deal").[[16]](#cite_note-17)

The plan was divided into three parts: one of them, the [American Rescue Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Rescue_Plan_Act_of_2021 "American Rescue Plan Act of 2021"), a COVID-19 relief spending bill, was signed into law in March 2021.[[17]](#cite_note-:22-18) The other two parts were reworked into different bills over the course of extensive negotiations within and among Congressional entities. The American Jobs Plan (AJP) was a proposal to address long-neglected infrastructure needs and reduce America's contributions to [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change")'s destructive effects;[[18]](#cite_note-:02-19) the American Families Plan (AFP) was a proposal to fund a variety of [social policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_policy "Social policy") initiatives, some of which (e.g. paid [family leave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_leave "Family leave")) had never before been enacted nationally in the U.S.[[19]](#cite_note-20)

The [Build Back Better Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Build_Back_Better_Act "Build Back Better Act") was a [bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_(law) "Bill (law)") introduced in the [117th Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/117th_United_States_Congress "117th United States Congress") to fulfill aspects of the [Build Back Better Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Build_Back_Better_Plan "Build Back Better Plan"). It was spun off from the American Jobs Plan, alongside the [Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrastructure_Investment_and_Jobs_Act "Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act"), as a $3.5 trillion [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") [reconciliation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconciliation_(United_States_Congress) "Reconciliation (United States Congress)") package that included provisions related to [climate change in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change_in_the_United_States "Climate change in the United States") (centered around Senator [Ron Wyden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Wyden "Ron Wyden")'s technology-neutral, tax incentive-first approach)[[20]](#cite_note-Dayen_on_Wyden_2022-21)[[21]](#cite_note-Weissmann_2023-22) and [social policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_policy "Social policy"), lowered to approximately $2.2 trillion. The bill was passed 220–213 by the [House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") on November 19, 2021.

In December 2021, amidst negotiations and [parliamentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentarian_of_the_United_States_Senate "Parliamentarian of the United States Senate") procedures, Senator [Joe Manchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Manchin "Joe Manchin") publicly pulled his support from the bill citing its cost and a too-aggressive transition to clean energy,[[22]](#cite_note-23) then retracted support for his own compromise legislation. The [United States](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") has supported [Ukraine](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine") during the ongoing [Russo-Ukrainian war](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Ukrainian_war "Russo-Ukrainian war"). The [Russian invasion of Ukraine](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine"), which began in February 2022, was condemned by the [Biden administration](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biden_administration "Biden administration"), which provided [military](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_military_aid_to_Ukraine_during_the_Russo-Ukrainian_War "List of military aid to Ukraine during the Russo-Ukrainian War"), financial, and [humanitarian](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_humanitarian_aid_to_Ukraine_during_the_Russo-Ukrainian_War "List of humanitarian aid to Ukraine during the Russo-Ukrainian War") aid to Ukraine, and imposed [sanctions](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_sanctions_during_the_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "International sanctions during the Russian invasion of Ukraine") against [Russia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia") and [Belarus](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belarus "Belarus").[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) However, the [second Trump administration](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Trump_administration "Second Trump administration") since 2025 has proposed a peace deal and increasingly sought to distance itself from financially supporting Ukrainian resistance.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

From January 2022 to December 2024, according to the [Kiel Institute](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiel_Institute "Kiel Institute"), the United States has provided around half of all military aid to Ukraine and has spent $119.7 billion on activities related to the Russian invasion,[[4]](#cite_note-:6-4)[[5]](#cite_note-:2-5) and on other activities including supporting increased US–European presence, Ukrainian refugees in the US, and global food insecurity.[[6]](#cite_note-:5-6) According to the [Council on Foreign Relations](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_on_Foreign_Relations "Council on Foreign Relations"), by the end of September 2024 the United States had allocated $175 billion, related to the invasion of Russia, $106 billion of which went into direct aid to Ukraine, whilst $69 billion remained in the US economy to support US industries.[[7]](#cite_note-CFR-7)[[8]](#cite_note-Lawfare-8)

There are several ways by which the US provides military and financial aid to Ukraine. Most of the military aid is old American weaponry and equipment from US [reserve stockpiles](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_reserve_stock "War reserve stock"); Presidential Drawdown Authority (PDA) allows the president to order the sending of this weaponry. American military contractors are then funded to make weapons to re-fill stockpiles.[[8]](#cite_note-Lawfare-8) The [Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine_Security_Assistance_Initiative "Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative") (USAI) funds the US Department of Defense to help train and advise the Ukrainian military, as well as to procure weaponry and equipment.[[8]](#cite_note-Lawfare-8) The State Department's [Foreign Military Financing](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Military_Financing "Foreign Military Financing") (FMF) program helps allies like Ukraine buy weaponry and equipment from American manufacturers.[[8]](#cite_note-Lawfare-8) Lastly, the US also sent some direct financial aid to the Ukrainian government through the [United States Agency for International Development](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Agency_for_International_Development "United States Agency for International Development") (USAID).[[8]](#cite_note-Lawfare-8)

The Biden administration also imposed limits on the supply and use of some American weapons. For more than two years, it forbade Ukraine to fire American weapons, like the [Army Tactical Missile System](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_Tactical_Missile_System "Army Tactical Missile System") (ATACMS), at military targets inside Russia.[[8]](#cite_note-Lawfare-8) From June 2024, it allowed Ukraine to strike inside Russia with US-supplied weapons, but only near the border in self-defense.[[9]](#cite_note-9) On March 3, 2025, following disagreements during the [2025 Trump–Zelenskyy meeting](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Trump–Zelenskyy_meeting "2025 Trump–Zelenskyy meeting"), the second Trump administration paused all military aid to Ukraine.[[10]](#cite_note-10) However, on March 11, 2025, U.S. military aid to Ukraine resumed after Ukraine agreed to a potential ceasefire.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

## Biden administration (2022–2025)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/President_Biden_on_2022_Russia_invasion.webm/330px--President_Biden_on_2022_Russia_invasion.webm.jpg)](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d3/President_Biden_on_2022_Russia_invasion.webm)

US President [Joe Biden](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") gives his remarks on the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

The Biden administration got information on a potential Russian invasion as early as March 2021, at the time of large Russian military exercises.[*[citation needed](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] The US attempted to deter Russia from invading by proposing US – Russia summit, and meeting with Russian officials in November 2021 and January 2022. The efforts failed.[[12]](#cite_note-War_in_Ukraine:_Conflict_2024-12)

### Strategy

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Joint_press_conference_President_Biden_and_President_Volodymyr_Zelenskyy.jpg/250px-Joint_press_conference_President_Biden_and_President_Volodymyr_Zelenskyy.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Joint_press_conference_President_Biden_and_President_Volodymyr_Zelenskyy.jpg)

Biden and Zelenskyy hold a press conference in the [East Room](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Room "East Room") of the [White House](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House"), December 21, 2022.

Since the start of the Russian invasion in 2022, US President Joe Biden has articulated a cautious US strategy towards the war. The goals were to mitigate the risk of escalation into a direct US-Russia confrontation while hindering Russia's military success. The Biden administration emphasized sustained support "for as long as it takes" to assist Ukraine's defense efforts. However, these are coupled with a focus on avoiding actions that could be construed as provocative by Russia and potentially leading to a wider war.[[12]](#cite_note-War_in_Ukraine:_Conflict_2024-12)

This cautious approach prioritizes limiting US risks of getting militarily involved while leaving the primary burden of repelling the invasion on Ukraine. [Political scientist](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_scientist "Political scientist") [Kori Schake](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kori_Schake "Kori Schake") characterizes this strategy as exhibiting a "vulnerability of US support", arguing that the self-imposed limitations on US assistance, compared to Russia's aggression not limited by any boundaries, create a significant strategic advantage for Russia.[[12]](#cite_note-War_in_Ukraine:_Conflict_2024-12)

While this US strategy has been static for 2 years of war, the situation on the battlefield was changing with time. Eventually, static US strategy encountered its limitations. As the war enters its third year (as of April 2024), the battlefield situation evolved towards a stalemate and towards increased concerns that a persistent and determined Russian offensive could ultimately achieve its objectives.[[12]](#cite_note-War_in_Ukraine:_Conflict_2024-12)

In May 2023, Russia's Security Council Secretary [Nikolai Patrushev](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolai_Patrushev "Nikolai Patrushev") accused the United States of involvement in Ukrainian attacks inside Russia.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/39/President_Joe_Biden_shakes_hands_with_Ukrainian_President_Volodymyr_Zelenskyy_during_the_NATO_Summit_in_Washington%2C_D.C._on_11_July_2024_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-President_Joe_Biden_shakes_hands_with_Ukrainian_President_Volodymyr_Zelenskyy_during_the_NATO_Summit_in_Washington%2C_D.C._on_11_July_2024_%28cropped%29.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:President_Joe_Biden_shakes_hands_with_Ukrainian_President_Volodymyr_Zelenskyy_during_the_NATO_Summit_in_Washington,_D.C._on_11_July_2024_(cropped).jpg)

Biden and Zelenskyy at the [2024 NATO Summit](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Washington_summit "2024 Washington summit") in Washington, D.C., July 11, 2024

The Biden administration reportedly told Ukraine to stop attacking [oil refineries in Russia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum_industry_in_Russia "Petroleum industry in Russia"), believing it would raise world energy prices and bring more aggressive Russian retaliation.[[14]](#cite_note-14) The US also expressed concern at a Ukrainian drone strike against a Russian nuclear [early-warning radar](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early-warning_radar "Early-warning radar"), believing that it could dangerously unsettle the Russian government.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

In May 2024, Biden gave Ukraine permission to [strike targets inside Russia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attacks_in_Russia_during_the_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "Attacks in Russia during the Russian invasion of Ukraine") adjacent to the [Kharkiv region](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kharkiv_region "Kharkiv region") of Ukraine using American-supplied weapons.[[16]](#cite_note-16) On August 9, 2024, U.S.-supplied [HIMARS](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIMARS "HIMARS") rocket system [destroyed](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_2024_Kursk_Oblast_incursion "August 2024 Kursk Oblast incursion") a convoy of Russian troops in the [Kursk Oblast](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kursk_Oblast "Kursk Oblast") of Russia in what Russian milbloggers described as one of the bloodiest attacks of the entire war.[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18)

In September 2024, Russian president [Vladimir Putin](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Putin "Vladimir Putin") threatened retaliation for attacks on Russian territory with weapons supplied by the United States and its NATO allies.[[19]](#cite_note-19)[[20]](#cite_note-20) U.S. officials did not believe that Ukraine had enough ATACMS and British [Storm Shadow](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Shadow "Storm Shadow") missiles to alter the course of the war, according to *The New York Times*.[[21]](#cite_note-21) On November 17, 2024, the Biden administration authorized the use of long-range [ATACMS](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ATACMS "ATACMS") missiles for military targets inside mainland Russia.[[22]](#cite_note-22)[[23]](#cite_note-23)

In the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), [abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion "Abortion") is a divisive issue in [politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_politics "American politics") and [culture wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_war "Culture war"). Prior to the mid-19th century, English [common law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_law "Common law") formed the basis of abortion law in the colonies and the early Republic.

Connecticut was the first state to regulate abortion in 1821; it outlawed abortion after quickening, the moment in pregnancy when the pregnant woman starts to feel the fetus's movement in the uterus, and forbade the use of poisons to induce one post-quickening. Many states subsequently passed various laws on abortion until the [Supreme Court of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") decisions of *[Roe v. Wade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roe_v._Wade "Roe v. Wade")* and *[Doe v. Bolton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doe_v._Bolton "Doe v. Bolton")* decriminalized abortion nationwide in 1973. The *Roe* decision imposed a federally mandated uniform framework for state legislation on the subject. It also established a minimal period during which abortion is legal, with more or fewer restrictions throughout the pregnancy.

That basic framework, modified in *[Planned Parenthood v. Casey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_Parenthood_v._Casey "Planned Parenthood v. Casey")* (1992), remained nominally in place, although the effective availability of abortion varied significantly from state to state, as many counties had no abortion providers.[[1]](#cite_note-Doan3-5) *Casey* held that a law could not place legal restrictions imposing an "[undue burden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undue_burden "Undue burden")" for "the purpose or effect of placing a substantial obstacle in the path of a woman seeking an abortion of a nonviable fetus."[[2]](#cite_note-6) In December 2021, the [FDA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration "Food and Drug Administration") legalized [telemedicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telemedicine "Telemedicine") provision of medication abortion pills with delivery by mail, but many states have laws which restrict this option.

In 2022, *Roe* and *Casey* were overturned in *[Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobbs_v._Jackson_Women's_Health_Organization "Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization")*, ending protection of abortion rights by the [United States Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Constitution "United States Constitution") and allowing individual states to regulate any aspect of abortion not preempted by federal law.[[3]](#cite_note-7) Since 1976, the [Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") has generally sought to restrict abortion access based on the stage of pregnancy or to criminalize abortion, whereas the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") has generally defended access to abortion and has made [contraception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_control_in_the_United_States "Birth control in the United States") easier to obtain.[[4]](#cite_note-8)

The [abortion-rights movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_abortion-rights_movement "United States abortion-rights movement") advocates for patient choice and bodily autonomy, while the [anti-abortion movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_anti-abortion_movement "United States anti-abortion movement") advocate that the fetus has a [right to live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_to_live "Right to live"). Historically [framed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Framing_(social_sciences) "Framing (social sciences)") as a debate between the [pro-choice and pro-life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro-choice_and_pro-life "Pro-choice and pro-life") labels, most Americans agree with some positions of each side.[[5]](#cite_note-9) Support for abortion gradually increased in the U.S. beginning in the early 1970s,[[6]](#cite_note-:02-10) and stabilized during the 2010s.[[7]](#cite_note-:2-11)[[8]](#cite_note-Gallup2018-12) The abortion rate has continuously declined from a peak in 1980 of 30 per 1,000 women of childbearing age (15–44) to 11.3 by 2018.[[9]](#cite_note-Abortion_Surveillance_—_United_States,_2018-13) In 2018, 78% of abortions were performed at 9 weeks or less gestation, and 92% of abortions were performed at 13 weeks or less gestation.[[9]](#cite_note-Abortion_Surveillance_—_United_States,_2018-13) By 2023, [medication abortions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medication_abortion "Medication abortion") accounted for 63% of all abortions.[[10]](#cite_note-Guttmacher_2024-03-19-14) Almost 25% of women will have had an abortion by age 45, with 20% of 30 year olds having had one.[[11]](#cite_note-Guttmacher_2017-10-19-15) In 2019, 60% of women who had abortions were already mothers, and 50% already had two or more children.[[12]](#cite_note-NYT_2021-12-14-16)[[13]](#cite_note-Parenting_2022-06-24-17) Increased access to [birth control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_control "Birth control") has been statistically linked to reductions in the abortion rate.[[14]](#cite_note-ObGyn_2012_No-Cost_Contraception-18)[[15]](#cite_note-Guttmacher_2016_Drop_in_Unintended-19)[[16]](#cite_note-Brookings_2019_Access_to_Contraception-20) The first state to decriminalize abortion prior to *Roe* was [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_in_Hawaii "Abortion in Hawaii").[[17]](#cite_note-Medicine:_Abortion_on_Request-21)[[18]](#cite_note-Abor_HI-22)[[19]](#cite_note-23)[[20]](#cite_note-:42-24)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/1999-_Gun-related_deaths_USA.svg/330px-1999-_Gun-related_deaths_USA.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1999-_Gun-related_deaths_USA.svg)

Gun-related suicides and homicides in the United States[[1]](#cite_note-NSC-CDC-1)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Gun_deaths_in_U.S._Venn_Diagram.png/330px-Gun_deaths_in_U.S._Venn_Diagram.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gun_deaths_in_U.S._Venn_Diagram.png)

Gun deaths in U.S. in proportional relationship to total population (2012 analysis, based on 2008 data)

Tens of thousands of firearms-related deaths and injuries occur in the United States each year.[[2]](#cite_note-NAS-exec-2)
Data are collected yearly by the [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention"), the [US Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Department_of_Justice "US Department of Justice") Bureau of Justice Statistics, the [FBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI "FBI"), and various state and local agencies.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5) In 2023, the CDC reported 46,728 gun deaths, of which 58% were [suicides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicide "Suicide"), 38% were [homicides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homicide "Homicide"), and the remainder were categorized as [law enforcement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_enforcement "Law enforcement") related, [accidental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accidental_death "Accidental death"), or of undetermined cause.[[6]](#cite_note-6) In 2024, firearm deaths fell to 44,447; suicides accounted for 62% of firearm deaths, homicides accounted for 35%, and the remainder involved law enforcement, were accidental, or had undetermined circumstances.[[7]](#cite_note-7) Preliminary data for 2025 indicated continued declines in homicides and non-suicide shooting deaths, though final CDC firearm mortality data for 2025 had not yet been released.[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9)

In 2023, 350 shootings occurred in K-12 schools with an additional 30 on college campuses. This marked the highest number of shootings recorded on school grounds.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

According to a [Pew Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pew_Research_Center "Pew Research Center") report, gun deaths among America's children rose 50% from 2019 to 2021.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

Estimates of defensive gun use in the United States vary widely and are contested.[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13) Analyses of the U.S. Bureau of Justice Statistics' National Crime Victimization Survey—a large, ongoing probability survey that first establishes that a crime occurred—indicate roughly 61,000–65,000 firearm defenses per year across 1987–2021.[[14]](#cite_note-14) An online survey of gun owners in 2021 returned a higher figure.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

Legislation at the [federal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States "Federal government of the United States"), state, and local levels has attempted to address gun violence through methods including restricting firearms purchases by youths and other "at-risk" populations, setting waiting periods for firearm purchases, establishing [gun buyback programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun_buyback_program "Gun buyback program"), law enforcement and policing strategies, stiff sentencing of gun law violators, education programs for parents and children, and community outreach programs.

Recent polling suggests up to 26% of Americans believe guns are the number one national public health threat.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/1970-_Gun_production_-_US.svg/330px-1970-_Gun_production_-_US.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1970-_Gun_production_-_US.svg)

Annual gun production in the U.S. has increased substantially in the 21st century, after having remained fairly level over preceding decades.[[17]](#cite_note-TheTrace_20240409-17) By 2023, a majority of U.S. states allowed adults to carry concealed guns in public.[[17]](#cite_note-TheTrace_20240409-17)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/2000-_Gun_sales_and_NICS_firearm_background_checks_-_U.S.svg/330px-2000-_Gun_sales_and_NICS_firearm_background_checks_-_U.S.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2000-_Gun_sales_and_NICS_firearm_background_checks_-_U.S.svg)

Estimated U.S. gun sales have risen in the 21st century, peaking in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.[[18]](#cite_note-TheTrace_thru2025-18) "NICS" is the FBI's National Instant Background Check System.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Map._Percent_of_households_with_guns_by_US_state_in_2016._RAND_Corporation.svg/330px-Map._Percent_of_households_with_guns_by_US_state_in_2016._RAND_Corporation.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Map._Percent_of_households_with_guns_by_US_state_in_2016._RAND_Corporation.svg)

Percent of households with guns in 2016. [RAND Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAND_Corporation "RAND Corporation").[[19]](#cite_note-RAND-19)[[20]](#cite_note-RAND-2-20)

The [Congressional Research Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Research_Service "Congressional Research Service") in 2009 estimated that among US population of 306 million people, there were 310 million firearms in the U.S., not including military armaments. Of these, 114 million were handguns, 110 million were rifles, and 86 million were shotguns.[[21]](#cite_note-21)[[22]](#cite_note-22)
Accurate figures for civilian gun ownership are difficult to determine.[[23]](#cite_note-conundrum-23) The percentage of Americans and American households who claim to own guns has been in long-term decline, according to the [General Social Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Social_Survey "General Social Survey") poll. It found that gun ownership by households may have declined from about half, in the late 1970s and early 1980s, down to 32% in 2015. The percentage of individual owners may have declined from 31% in 1985 to 22% in 2014.[[24]](#cite_note-24)

Gun ownership figures are generally estimated via polling, by such organizations as the [General Social Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Social_Survey "General Social Survey") (GSS), [Harris Interactive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_Insights_&_Analytics "Harris Insights & Analytics"), and [Gallup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallup_(company) "Gallup (company)"). There are significant disparities in the results across polls by different organizations, calling into question their reliability.[[25]](#cite_note-25) In Gallup's 1972 survey, 43% reported having a gun in their home. GSS's 1973 survey resulted in 49% reporting a gun in the home. In 1993, Gallup's poll results were 51%. GSS's 1994 poll showed 43%.[[26]](#cite_note-Pew-26) In 2012, Gallup's survey showed 47% of Americans reporting having a gun in their home,[[27]](#cite_note-Gallup-27) while the GSS in 2012 reports 34%.[[26]](#cite_note-Pew-26) In 2018 it was estimated that [U.S. civilians own 393 million firearms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_gun_ownership "American gun ownership"),[[28]](#cite_note-28) and that 40% to 42% of the households in the country have at least one gun. However, record gun sales followed in the subsequent years.[[29]](#cite_note-29)[[30]](#cite_note-30)[[31]](#cite_note-31)

In 1997, estimates were about 44 million gun owners in the United States. These owners possessed around 192 million firearms, of which an estimated 65 million were handguns.[[32]](#cite_note-Cook-Ludwig1997-32) A National Survey on Private Ownership and Use of Firearms (NSPOF), conducted in 1994, estimated that Americans owned 192 million guns: 36% rifles, 34% handguns, 26% shotguns, and 4% other types of long guns.[[32]](#cite_note-Cook-Ludwig1997-32) Most firearm owners owned multiple firearms, with the NSPOF survey indicating 25% of adults owned firearms.[[32]](#cite_note-Cook-Ludwig1997-32) Throughout the 1970s and much of the 1980s, the estimated rate of gun ownership in the home ranged from 45 to 50%.[[26]](#cite_note-Pew-26) After highly publicized mass murders, it is consistently observed that there are rapid increases in gun purchases and large crowds at gun vendors and gun shows, due to fears of increased gun control .[[33]](#cite_note-33)[[34]](#cite_note-34)[[35]](#cite_note-35)[[36]](#cite_note-36)[[37]](#cite_note-37)

Gun ownership rates vary across geographic regions, ranging from 2004 estimates of 25% in the [Northeastern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeastern_United_States "Northeastern United States") to 60% in the [East South Central States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_South_Central_States "East South Central States").[[38]](#cite_note-azrael-2004-38) A 2004 [Gallup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallup_(company) "Gallup (company)") poll estimated that 49% of men reported gun ownership, compared to 33% of women, while 44% of whites owned a gun, compared to 24% of nonwhites.[[39]](#cite_note-Gallup_2004-39) An estimated 56% of those living in rural areas owned a gun, compared to 40% of suburbanites and 29% of those in urban areas.[[39]](#cite_note-Gallup_2004-39) Approximately 53% of Republicans owned guns, compared to 36% of political independents and 31% of Democrats.[[39]](#cite_note-Gallup_2004-39)

One criticism of the GSS survey and other proxy measures of gun ownership, is that they do not provide adequate macro-level detail to allow conclusions on the relationship between overall firearm ownership and gun violence.[[40]](#cite_note-NAS-ch3-40) [Gary Kleck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Kleck "Gary Kleck") compared various survey and proxy measures and found no correlation between overall firearm ownership and gun violence.[[41]](#cite_note-Kleck-20

The **Bipartisan Safer Communities Act** is a [United States federal law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_the_United_States "Law of the United States") passed by the [117th United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/117th_United_States_Congress "117th United States Congress") in 2022. It implemented several changes to the [mental health system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare_in_the_United_States#Mental_health "Healthcare in the United States"), [school safety programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_security "School security"), and [gun control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun_control "Gun control") laws. Gun control laws in the bill include extended [background checks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Background_check "Background check") for firearm purchasers under the age of 21, clarification of [federal firearms license](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_firearms_license "Federal firearms license") (FFL) requirements, funding for state [red flag laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_flag_law "Red flag law") and other [crisis intervention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_intervention "Crisis intervention") programs, further criminalization of [arms trafficking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arms_trafficking "Arms trafficking") and [straw purchases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straw_purchase "Straw purchase"), and partial closure of the [gun show loophole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun_show_loophole "Gun show loophole")[[1]](#cite_note-1) and [boyfriend loophole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyfriend_loophole "Boyfriend loophole"). It was the first federal gun control legislation enacted in two decades.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

The bill was introduced by Senator [Marco Rubio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Rubio "Marco Rubio") ([R](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)")–[FL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida")) on October 5, 2021, as an unrelated bill, then modified by an amendment by Senator [Chris Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Murphy "Chris Murphy") ([D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)")–[CT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut "Connecticut")) on June 21, 2022, and signed into law by President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") on June 25, 2022.

On March 27, 2023, a [mass shooting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_shooting "Mass shooting") occurred at The Covenant School, a [Presbyterian Church in America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_in_America "Presbyterian Church in America") parochial elementary school in the [Green Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Hills,_Nashville,_Tennessee "Green Hills, Nashville, Tennessee") neighborhood of [Nashville, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville,_Tennessee "Nashville, Tennessee"), United States, when 28-year-old Aiden Hale killed three nine‑year‑old children and three adults before officer Rex Engelbert and detective Michael Collazo, members of the [Metropolitan Nashville Police Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Nashville_Police_Department "Metropolitan Nashville Police Department") (MNPD) shot and killed him. Hale was a former student of the school who had been planning the attack for years.[[9]](#cite_note-Kallingal_et_al.-11)[[10]](#cite_note-12)[[11]](#cite_note-NY_Times_2023-03-28-13) It is the [deadliest school shooting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_school_shootings_in_the_United_States_by_death_toll "List of school shootings in the United States by death toll") in [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee") history.

In April 2025, the MNPD closed its investigation into the shooting, concluding that Hale had been motivated by numerous factors, including a desire for notoriety and media attention.[[12]](#cite_note-14)[[13]](#cite_note-:0-15) Hale had chosen The Covenant School because he considered the years he attended the school to be the happiest of his life and he wanted to die somewhere that made him happy.[[14]](#cite_note-Prepared_For_Years-16)[[15]](#cite_note-Motive_Revealed-17)

The Covenant School's campus pictured in October 2023

The Covenant School is a [private](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_school "Private school") [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_school "Christian school") school in the Green Hills neighborhood of Nashville. It educates students from pre-kindergarten to the sixth grade. It was founded in 2001 as a ministry of Nashville's Covenant Presbyterian Church, a congregation of the [Presbyterian Church in America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_in_America "Presbyterian Church in America"); its enrollment is about 200 students.[[16]](#cite_note-CNN_2023-03-27-18)

## Shooting

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/2023_Nashville_School_Shooting_CCTV_Footage.webm/250px-seek%3D117-2023_Nashville_School_Shooting_CCTV_Footage.webm.jpg)](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d3/2023_Nashville_School_Shooting_CCTV_Footage.webm)

[CCTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CCTV "CCTV") footage released by Nashville Police showing Hale entering and walking throughout the school armed during the shooting

On the morning of March 27, 2023, Hale drove to The Covenant School, arriving at 9:54 a.m. [CDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Time_Zone "Central Time Zone").[[17]](#cite_note-USAToday_Timeline-19)[[18]](#cite_note-WSMV_2023-03-27-20) At 9:57, Hale sent an [Instagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instagram "Instagram") message to an old friend saying an earlier post was "basically a suicide note" and anticipating dying that day.[[19]](#cite_note-21) The friend who received the message called a [crisis hotline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_hotline "Crisis hotline"), then contacted the Davidson County Sheriff's Office at 10:13.[[20]](#cite_note-22)

At 10:10, Hale, armed with an [AR-15-style pistol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-15%E2%80%93style_pistol "AR-15–style pistol"), a [KelTec SUB-2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KelTec_SUB-2000 "KelTec SUB-2000"), and a [handgun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handgun "Handgun"), shot through a set of glass side doors and entered the building.[[21]](#cite_note-NYT_2023-03-27-23)[[22]](#cite_note-Guardian_2023-03-27-24)[[23]](#cite_note-25) A school custodian noticed Hale shooting his way into the school and tried to run away, but was immediately shot to death. The smoke from the gunfire triggered the fire alarm, causing staff members and students to initiate an evacuation without knowing there was an active shooter.

Hale then went up to the second floor, and at the top of the stairwell encountered a [substitute teacher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Substitute_teacher "Substitute teacher") and several children who were about to go downstairs; Hale fired at them with the AR-pistol, fatally shooting three children and the substitute teacher. The other evacuating students and staff escaped unharmed and barricaded themselves inside their classrooms. Hale then walked up to the four victims and fired more shots into them while walking into the second-floor hallway. On the second floor, Hale fired into two adjacent classrooms, emptying two magazines in the process and injuring one student in one of the rooms. Hale then stopped shooting and reloaded while continuing to search for potential victims in the second-floor hallway. Hearing the fire alarms go off, the school's headmaster exited her office on the second floor, unaware that an active shooter incident was happening. Hale rounded the corner from the church offices into the same hallway and encountered the headmaster, who asked Hale what he was doing. Hale responded by shooting her multiple times with his AR-pistol, then walked up to the headmaster and shot her once more with his handgun.

After this point, Hale spent the next three minutes searching for potential victims in the rooms near the headmaster's body, and during this time also switched to the carbine. After failing to find anyone Hale backtracked to the church offices, where several faculty members were hiding, and was also unsuccessful at finding potential victims in this area. At 10:19, Hale went downstairs and headed to the church sanctuary, near the entrance of which he shot at two television sets with his carbine. He then fired through the double doors leading to the Pre-K and Kindergarten classrooms without hitting anyone, before returning upstairs and entering the emptied-out church sanctuary, where he fired seven times at a [stained-glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stained_glass "Stained glass") window depicting [Adam and Eve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_and_Eve "Adam and Eve") with his carbine before leaving. Hale then walked by a window at the church [vestibule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestibule_(architecture) "Vestibule (architecture)") and noticed police cars arriving. Switching back to his AR-pistol, Hale fired through the window at the officers outside for over two minutes. No officers were hit by gunfire, but two police vehicles were disabled.[[13]](#cite_note-:0-15)[[24]](#cite_note-26)[[25]](#cite_note-27)

The score ranges are:

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| **Less corrupt**   90–100    80–89    70–79    60–69    50–59 | **More corrupt**   40–49    30–39    20–29    10–19    0–9    No data |



The **Corruption Perceptions Index** (**CPI**) is an index published annually by [Transparency International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transparency_International "Transparency International"), a German [registered association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Registered_association_(Germany) "Registered association (Germany)"), since 1995.[[1]](#cite_note-1) It scores and ranks countries by their perceived levels of [public sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_sector "Public sector")[[2]](#cite_note-cpi-2) [corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corruption "Corruption"), as assessed by experts and business executives.[[3]](#cite_note-3) The CPI generally defines corruption as an "abuse of entrusted power for private gain".[[4]](#cite_note-cpilong-4): 2

From 1995 to 2011, the index was scored on a scale of 10 to 0. Since 2012, the Corruption Perceptions Index has been ranked on a scale from 100 (very clean) to 0 (highly corrupt).

Of the 182 countries ranked in the 2025 CPI, published in February 2026, the top scorers included [Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark "Denmark") (89), [Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland "Finland") (88), and [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore") (84), while those perceived as the most corrupt included [South Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sudan "South Sudan") (9), [Somalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somalia "Somalia") (9), and [Venezuela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venezuela "Venezuela") (10).[[5]](#cite_note-ti_2025-5)

Although widely used as a key indicator of corruption, the CPI does not capture all forms of corruption. Perceptions about corruption may differ from actual levels of corruption and the index focuses solely on the public sector. For a more comprehensive picture, the CPI should be used alongside other assessments.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

The CPI methodology, revised in 2012, enables consistent comparison of corruption perceptions across countries and years. It involves four stages: selecting data sources, rescaling them to a uniform 0–100 scale, aggregating the results, and estimating uncertainty.[[4]](#cite_note-cpilong-4): 7

### Selection of source data

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Corruption_Perceptions_Index&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Selection of source data")]

The goal of the data selection is to capture expert and business leader assessments of various public sector corruption practices. This includes [bribery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bribery "Bribery"), misuse of public funds, abuse of public office for personal gain, [nepotism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepotism "Nepotism") in civil service, and [state capture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_capture "State capture"). Since 2012 CPI has taken into account 13 different surveys and assessments[[7]](#cite_note-7) from 12 different institutions.[[4]](#cite_note-cpilong-4): 1 The institutions are:

* [African Development Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Development_Bank "African Development Bank") (based in Ivory Coast)
* [Bertelsmann Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertelsmann_Foundation "Bertelsmann Foundation") (based in Germany)
* [Economist Intelligence Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economist_Intelligence_Unit "Economist Intelligence Unit") (based in the UK)
* [Freedom House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_House "Freedom House") (based in the US)
* [Global Insight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Insight "Global Insight") (based in the US)
* [International Institute for Management Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Institute_for_Management_Development "International Institute for Management Development") (based in Switzerland)
* Political and Economic Risk Consultancy (based in Hong Kong)
* The PRS Group, Inc. (based in the US)
* [World Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank "World Bank")
* [World Economic Forum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Economic_Forum "World Economic Forum")
* [World Justice Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Justice_Project "World Justice Project") (based in the US)

Countries need to be evaluated by at least three sources to appear in the CPI.[[4]](#cite_note-cpilong-4): 7 The CPI measures the perception of corruption due to the difficulty of measuring absolute levels of corruption.[[8]](#cite_note-cpifaq-8)
[Transparency International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transparency_International "Transparency International") commissioned the [University of Passau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Passau "University of Passau")'s [Johann Graf Lambsdorff](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann%20Graf%20Lambsdorff "de:Johann Graf Lambsdorff") to produce the CPI.[[9]](#cite_note-2005FAQ-9) Early CPIs used public opinion surveys.[[4]](#cite_note-cpilong-4): 7

### Rescaling source data

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Corruption_Perceptions_Index&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Rescaling source data")]

In order for all data to be aggregated into the CPI, it is first necessary to carry out standardization during which all data points are converted to a scale of 0–100. Here, 0 represents the most corruption and 100 signifies the least. Indices originally measuring corruption inversely (higher values for higher corruption) are multiplied by -1 to align with the 0–100 scale.

In the next step, the [mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean "Mean") and [standard deviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_deviation "Standard deviation") for each data source based on data from the baseline year are calculated (the "impute" command of the [STATA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STATA "STATA") statistical software package is used to replace missing values). Subsequently, a standardized [z score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z_score "Z score") is calculated with an average centered around 0 and a standard deviation of 1 for each source from each country. Finally, these scores are converted back to a 0–100 scale with a mean of approximately 45 and a standard deviation of 20. Scores below 0 are set to 0, and scores exceeding 100 are capped at 100. This ensures consistent comparability across years since 2012.

### Aggregating the rescaled data

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Corruption_Perceptions_Index&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Aggregating the rescaled data")]

The resulting CPI score for each country is calculated as a simple average of all its rescaled scores that are available for the given country, while at least three data sources must be available in order to calculate the index. The imputed data is used only for standardization and is not used as a score to calculate the index.

### Reporting a measure for uncertainty

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Corruption_Perceptions_Index&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Reporting a measure for uncertainty")]

The CPI score is accompanied by a [standard error](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_error "Standard error") and [confidence interval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confidence_interval "Confidence interval"). This reflects the variation present within the data sources used for a particular country or territory.

### CPI and economic growth

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Corruption_Perceptions_Index&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: CPI and economic growth")]

Research papers published in 2007 and 2008 examined the economic consequences of corruption perception, as defined by the CPI. The researchers found a correlation between a higher CPI and higher long-term economic growth,[[10]](#cite_note-10) as well as an increase in GDP growth of 1.7% for every unit increase in a country's CPI score.[[11]](#cite_note-11) Also shown was a [power-law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power-law "Power-law") dependence linking higher CPI score to higher rates of foreign investment in a country.

The research article "The Investigation of the Relationship between Corruption Perception Index and GDP in the Case of the Balkans"[[12]](#cite_note-12) from 2020 confirms the positive [co-integration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Co-integration "Co-integration") relationship in Balkan countries between CPI and GDP and calculates the affecting rate of CPI GDP as 0.34. Moreover, the direction of causality between CPI and GDP was identified from CPI to GDP and, according to this, the hypothesis that CPI is the cause of GDP was accepted.

The working paper *Corruption and Economic Growth: New Empirical Evidence*[[13]](#cite_note-13) from 2019 emphasizes that many previous studies used the CPI for their analysis before 2012 (when the index was difficult to compare over time) and therefore may be biased. At the same time, it presents new empirical evidence based on data for 175 over the period 2012–2018. The results show that corruption is negatively associated with economic growth (Real per capita GDP decreased by around 17% in the long-run when the reversed CPI increased by one standard deviation).

As reported by [Transparency International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transparency_International "Transparency International"), there is a correlation between the absence of [discrimination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrimination "Discrimination") and a better CPI score

**Robert Kyoung Hur** (born 1973) is an American lawyer who served as the [United States Attorney for the District of Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Attorney_for_the_District_of_Maryland "United States Attorney for the District of Maryland") from 2018 to 2021. He previously served as [Principal Associate Deputy Attorney General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_Associate_Deputy_Attorney_General "Principal Associate Deputy Attorney General") with the [U.S. Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Department_of_Justice "U.S. Department of Justice"). Hur oversaw the investigation into President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden")'s alleged [mishandling of classified documents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden_classified_documents_incident "Joe Biden classified documents incident") during Biden's time as [vice president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States "Vice President of the United States").

## Early life and education

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Robert_Hur&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Hur was born in 1973 in New York City to South Korean parents. His father, Young Hur, was an [anesthesiologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anesthesiology "Anesthesiology"), and his mother, Haesook Hur, worked as the office manager for her husband's anesthesiology practice.[[2]](#cite_note-US_Attorney-2)[[3]](#cite_note-:0-3)[[4]](#cite_note-:1-4) He was raised in Los Angeles where he attended the Harvard School (now [Harvard-Westlake School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard-Westlake_School "Harvard-Westlake School")).[[4]](#cite_note-:1-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Hur studied English and American literature at [Harvard College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_College "Harvard College"), graduating in 1995 with a [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts"), *[magna cum laude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magna_cum_laude "Magna cum laude")*. From 1995 to 1996, Hur did graduate study in philosophy at [King's College, Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_College,_Cambridge "King's College, Cambridge"), receiving [first-class honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-class_honours "First-class honours").[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) From 1996 to 1998, he worked for [Boston Consulting Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Consulting_Group "Boston Consulting Group"). He then attended [Stanford Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Law_School "Stanford Law School"), where he was the executive editor of the *[Stanford Law Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Law_Review "Stanford Law Review")* and won the school's Kirkwood Moot Court Competition. He graduated in 2001 with a [Juris Doctor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juris_Doctor "Juris Doctor") and membership in the [Order of the Coif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Coif "Order of the Coif").[[2]](#cite_note-US_Attorney-2)

After law school, Hur was a [law clerk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_clerk "Law clerk") for Judge [Alex Kozinski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Kozinski "Alex Kozinski") of the [U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Ninth_Circuit "United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit") from 2001 to 2002 and for Chief Justice [William Rehnquist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Rehnquist "William Rehnquist") of the [U.S. Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") from 2002 to 2003.[[2]](#cite_note-US_Attorney-2)

He then served as Special Assistant and Counsel to [Christopher A. Wray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_A._Wray "Christopher A. Wray"), then Assistant Attorney General in charge of the Justice Department's Criminal Division. From 2007 to 2014, he served as an [Assistant United States Attorney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assistant_United_States_Attorney "Assistant United States Attorney") in the District of Maryland, where he prosecuted gang violence, drug trafficking and firearms offenses, and white-collar crimes. He was a partner with [King & Spalding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_&_Spalding "King & Spalding") in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), where his practice focused on government investigations and complex litigation.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

### United States Attorney

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Robert_Hur&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: United States Attorney")]

Hur rejoined the Department of Justice as Principal [Associate Deputy Attorney General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associate_Deputy_Attorney_General "Associate Deputy Attorney General"), a top aide to [Rod Rosenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rod_Rosenstein "Rod Rosenstein") after Rosenstein became Deputy Attorney General. He was a liaison to Special Counsel [Robert Mueller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mueller "Robert Mueller")'s [investigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mueller_special_counsel_investigation "Mueller special counsel investigation") of Russian interference in the [2016 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_U.S._presidential_election "2016 U.S. presidential election").[[9]](#cite_note-9)

On November 1, 2017, Hur was nominated by President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") to be the next United States Attorney for the [District of Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_District_Court_for_the_District_of_Maryland "United States District Court for the District of Maryland").[[10]](#cite_note-10) On March 22, 2018, his nomination was reported out of committee by [voice vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voice_vote "Voice vote").[[11]](#cite_note-11) He was unanimously confirmed in the US Senate by voice vote later the same day.[[12]](#cite_note-12) He was sworn in on April 9, 2018.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

On November 2, 2022, Biden's attorneys discovered the first set of classified documents in a locked closet at the Penn Biden Center; they reported them that day to the [National Archives and Records Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archives_and_Records_Administration "National Archives and Records Administration") (NARA), which retrieved them the next day. CNN, quoting "former aides and others with direct knowledge of the process", reported that most of the actual packing of Biden's belongings and documents was done by lower-level staffers, though the staff had "clear Presidential Records Act guidelines" and took those guidelines seriously. The documents "not deemed covered by the records requirements to submit to the National Archives" were stored at a temporary facility run by the [General Services Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Services_Administration "General Services Administration") near the White House before eventually being moved to the Penn Biden Center.[[32]](#cite_note-32)

In October 2020, a controversy arose involving a laptop that belonged to [Hunter Biden](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunter_Biden "Hunter Biden"). The owner of a [Delaware](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware "Delaware") computer shop, John Paul Mac Isaac, said that the laptop had been left by a man who identified himself as Hunter Biden. Mac Isaac also stated that he is [legally blind](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legally_blind "Legally blind") and could not be sure whether the man was actually Hunter Biden.[[1]](#cite_note-Goldman_10/22/2020-1) Three weeks before the [2020 United States presidential election](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election "2020 United States presidential election"), the *[New York Post](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Post "New York Post")* published a front-page story that presented emails from the laptop, alleging they showed corruption by [Joe Biden](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden"), the Democratic presidential nominee and Hunter Biden's father.[[2]](#cite_note-MSN-2) According to the *Post*, the story was based on information provided to [Rudy Giuliani](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Giuliani "Rudy Giuliani"), the personal attorney of incumbent president and candidate [Donald Trump](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), by Mac Isaac.[[1]](#cite_note-Goldman_10/22/2020-1) Forensic analysis later authenticated some of the emails from the laptop, including both emails used by the *Post* in their initial reporting.[[7]](#cite_note-Authenticated-7)

Shortly after the *Post* story broke, social media companies blocked links to it, while other news outlets declined to publish the story due to concerns about provenance and suspicions of [Russian disinformation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_disinformation "Russian disinformation").[[8]](#cite_note-wapoMarch18-8) On October 19, 2020, an open letter signed by 51 former US intelligence officials warned that the laptop "has all the classic earmarks of a Russian information operation."[[9]](#cite_note-9) By May 2023, no evidence had publicly surfaced to support suspicions that the laptop was part of a Russian disinformation scheme.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11)

In December 2019, under the authority of a subpoena issued by a Wilmington grand jury, the FBI seized the laptop from Mac Isaac.[[1]](#cite_note-Goldman_10/22/2020-1)[[12]](#cite_note-Benner_Vogel_Schmidt_3/16/2022-12)[[13]](#cite_note-Goldman_Benner_Vogel_8/13/2020-13) FBI investigators handling Hunter Biden's laptop quickly concluded in 2019 "that the laptop was genuinely his and did not seem to have been tampered with or manipulated".[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-Stanage_6/29/2023-15) In June 2024, federal prosecutors utilized the laptop as evidence as part of a [criminal case](about://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunter_Biden#Firearms_trial_and_conviction "Hunter Biden") against Hunter Biden, alongside testimony from an FBI agent involved in authenticating and investigating the laptop.[[16]](#cite_note-abcjune4-16)

The hard drive data had been shared with Trump advisor [Steve Bannon](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Bannon "Steve Bannon") before it became publicly known.[[1]](#cite_note-Goldman_10/22/2020-1) Trump attempted to turn the story into an [October surprise](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_surprise "October surprise") to hurt Joe Biden's campaign by falsely alleging that, while in office, Biden had [acted corruptly regarding Ukraine](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biden–Ukraine_conspiracy_theory "Biden–Ukraine conspiracy theory") to protect his son.[[17]](#cite_note-Padden_10/28/2020-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18)[[19]](#cite_note-19) A joint investigation by two Republican Senate committees released in September 2020 and a [Republican House Oversight committee investigation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Oversight_Committee_investigation_into_the_Biden_family "United States House Oversight Committee investigation into the Biden family") released in April 2024 did not find wrongdoing by Joe Biden with regard to Ukraine and his son's business dealings there.[[25]](#cite_note-No_Wrongdoing-25) [PolitiFact](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PolitiFact "PolitiFact") wrote in June 2021 that the laptop did belong to Hunter Biden, but did not demonstrate wrongdoing by Joe Biden.[[26]](#cite_note-Drobnic-26)

Starting in 2021, news outlets began to authenticate some of the contents of the laptop. In 2021, *[Politico](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")* verified two key emails used in the *Post*'s initial reporting by cross-referencing emails with other datasets and contacting their recipients. It concluded that the "clean" data, including over 120,000 emails, originated with Hunter Biden and had not been altered, while other copies circulated by Republican operatives "could have been tampered with". Other outlets also verified portions of the data, while noting problems in fully authenticating the copies they had to work with.[[5]](#cite_note-Timberg_Viser_Hamburger_3/30/2022-5)[[4]](#cite_note-:5-4)[[3]](#cite_note-politico2021-3)

## Background

The media coverage of the laptop spurred speculation about the [Biden–Ukraine conspiracy theory](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biden–Ukraine_conspiracy_theory "Biden–Ukraine conspiracy theory"), which falsely[[27]](#cite_note-27) alleged that then vice president [Joe Biden](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") acted in Ukraine to protect his son from a corruption investigation by Ukrainian Prosecutor General [Viktor Shokin](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viktor_Shokin "Viktor Shokin"). On October 14, 2020, the *[New York Post](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Post "New York Post")* published an article based on an email from the laptop about a purported meeting between then vice president Joe Biden and the [Burisma](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burisma "Burisma") advisor Vadym Pozharskyi. The [Biden campaign](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden_2020_presidential_campaign "Joe Biden 2020 presidential campaign") denied Joe Biden had any meeting with Pozharskyi and said that if they had ever met, it would have been a brief encounter.[[28]](#cite_note-28) Witnesses at the dinner where they allegedly met said Joe Biden briefly passed by to see an old friend. The *Post* reported in its story that Pozharskyi declined to comment, and he did not comment to a *[Politico](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")* journalist who reported extensively on the story a year later.[[29]](#cite_note-29)

The *Post* reported that the email was found in a cache of data extracted from the [external hard drive](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/External_hard_drive "External hard drive") of a laptop computer that belonged to Hunter Biden. The *Post* reported that the repair shop owner had made a copy of the external hard drive before it was seized by the US [Federal Bureau of Investigation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation") (FBI) and that the copy was later provided to the *Post* by Donald Trump's attorney, [Rudy Giuliani](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Giuliani "Rudy Giuliani"). The subpoena to seize the laptop was issued by a grand jury on behalf of the US attorney's office in Wilmington, which was later reported to have been investigating Hunter Biden about lobbying and financial matters since at least 2018.[[1]](#cite_note-Goldman_10/22/2020-1)[[12]](#cite_note-Benner_Vogel_Schmidt_3/16/2022-12)
