The **2023 United Auto Workers strike** was a [labor strike](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_strike "Labor strike") involving automobile workers in the labor union [United Auto Workers](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Auto_Workers "United Auto Workers") (UAW) and the three unionized automakers in the United States—[Ford Motor Company](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Motor_Company "Ford Motor Company"), [General Motors](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Motors "General Motors"), and [Stellantis](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellantis "Stellantis"). These three automakers' factories combined employ about 145,000 UAW members and produce about 50 percent of the vehicles manufactured annually in the US, accounting for 1.5 percent of US [GDP](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product").[[3]](#cite_note-WSJ_2023-09-15-3)[[4]](#cite_note-WaPo_2023-09-15-4) The strike began on September 15, 2023, when the union was unable to reach a deal with the three automakers. It was the first trilateral strike against the three automakers in the union's history.

The hardline stance taken by the newly elected UAW president [Shawn Fain](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawn_Fain "Shawn Fain") contributed to the UAW's decision to strike. In particular, he has criticized stagnant wages that do not account for inflation and has called for the end of a tiered employment system that underpays newer employees, the restoration of overtime and retirement benefits that were lost due to the [2008 financial crisis](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis"), the institution of a [four-day workweek](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-day_workweek "Four-day workweek"), and improved worker protections against plant closures as [electric vehicle](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_vehicle "Electric vehicle") production increases.

A central concern for the automakers is the cost of labor relative to domestic and foreign non-union competitors, particularly as the industry transitions to electric vehicle manufacturing.[[5]](#cite_note-5) The automakers have stated that they anticipate the need to invest a significant portion of their profits from gasoline-powered vehicles into new production technology for electric vehicles.[[6]](#cite_note-NYT_2023-09-16-6)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2023_United_Auto_Workers_strike&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: United Auto Workers")]

The 1945—1946 strike established a strategy, forged by then-UAW president [Walter Reuther](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Reuther "Walter Reuther"), to target efforts on a single company. Since the 1950s, UAW has faced declining union membership and a growing service sector, reducing the economic impact that a strike could have.[[15]](#cite_note-15) In 2019, UAW autoworkers [went on strike](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_General_Motors_strike "2019 General Motors strike") against General Motors. The 40-day work stoppage cost General Motors US$3.6 billion and caused a single-quarter recession in [Michigan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan "Michigan").[[16]](#cite_note-16)

Fain called for [cost of living adjustments](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cost_of_living "Cost of living") to account for inflation ahead of the current contracts expiring on September 14 and asked for wage increases lost in the [2008 financial crisis](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis").[[17]](#cite_note-17) Members have expressed interest in both ending a two-tier wage system in which newer employees are paid significantly less than older employees, and domestic plant construction.[[18]](#cite_note-18) Fain continued his sentiments at the Automotive Press Association in April, expressing disappointment in the idling of the [Belvidere Assembly Plant](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belvidere_Assembly_Plant "Belvidere Assembly Plant") in [Belvidere, Illinois](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belvidere,_Illinois "Belvidere, Illinois").[[19]](#cite_note-19) Additionally, he lambasted wage decreases that workers at joint venture battery factories face compared to workers at older factories.[[20]](#cite_note-20)

By May 2023, the potential for a strike loomed over contract talks.[[21]](#cite_note-21) In an online appearance in June, Fain repeated his goals and criticized automobile manufacturers for increasing their profits without increasing wages.[[22]](#cite_note-22) Fain continued to leave strike action as a possible option leading up to contract negotiations.[[23]](#cite_note-23) Contract negotiations began on July 14.[[24]](#cite_note-24) Throughout negotiations, Fain has updated members online, including throwing one automaker's proposal in the trash on camera.[[25]](#cite_note-25) On August 15, Fain announced a strike vote;[[26]](#cite_note-26) it overwhelmingly passed on August 27 with 97 percent voting in favor.[[27]](#cite_note-27) UAW has asked for an immediate 20 percent raise and yearly gradual increases totaling an hourly pay increase of 46 percent, the restoration of traditional pension payment plans and retiree health care, a [four-day workweek](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-day_workweek "Four-day workweek"), job protections, and a beneficial transition to electric vehicles.[[28]](#cite_note-28) Fain has acknowledged the UAW demands are audacious but argues they are justified, pushing for the reversal of post-2007 wage cuts.[[29]](#cite_note-29)

The **2023 Hawaii wildfires** were a series of wildfires that broke out in early August 2023 in the [U.S. state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii "Hawaii"), predominantly on the island of [Maui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maui "Maui"). The wind-driven fires prompted evacuations and caused widespread damage, killing at least 102 people and leaving two people missing in the town of [Lahaina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahaina,_Hawaii "Lahaina, Hawaii") on Maui's northwest coast. The proliferation of the wildfires was attributed to dry, gusty conditions created by a strong [high-pressure area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-pressure_area "High-pressure area") north of Hawaii and [Hurricane Dora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Dora_(2023) "Hurricane Dora (2023)") to the south.[[11]](#cite_note-ABC-11)

An emergency declaration was signed on August 8, authorizing several actions, including activation of the [Hawaii National Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_National_Guard "Hawaii National Guard"), appropriate actions by the director of the [Hawaii Emergency Management Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_Emergency_Management_Agency "Hawaii Emergency Management Agency") and the Administrator of Emergency Management, and the expenditure of state general revenue funds for relief of conditions created by the fires.[[12]](#cite_note-:17-12) By August 9, the state government of Hawaii issued a [state of emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_emergency "State of emergency") for the entirety of the state.[[11]](#cite_note-ABC-11) On August 10, U.S. President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") issued a federal major disaster declaration.[[13]](#cite_note-CNN-13)

For the Lahaina fire alone, the [Pacific Disaster Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Disaster_Center "Pacific Disaster Center") (PDC) and the [Federal Emergency Management Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Emergency_Management_Agency "Federal Emergency Management Agency") (FEMA) estimated that over 2,200 buildings had been destroyed,[[5]](#cite_note-Lahaina_damage-5)[[14]](#cite_note-:5-14)[[15]](#cite_note-:9-15) overwhelmingly residential[[16]](#cite_note-:12-16)[[17]](#cite_note-:11-17) and including many historic landmarks in Lahaina.[[18]](#cite_note-18)[[19]](#cite_note-fatalities-19) The damage caused by the fire has been estimated at nearly $6 billion.[[5]](#cite_note-Lahaina_damage-5)[[20]](#cite_note-6billiondamage-20) In September 2023, the [United States Department of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Commerce "United States Department of Commerce") published the official damage total of the wildfires as $5.5 billion (2023 USD).[[6]](#cite_note-NOAA_Damage_Total-6)
